articles.body_html:
In a workforce calendar, shifts, absences, and days off can look like variations of the same event. They aren't. A day off belongs to a calendar date; a shift belongs to a span of time. Mixing those rules can move an event to the wrong day without producing an obvious error.

I worked on a workforce calendar using React, TypeScript, and Bryntum. It combined shifts, absences, overtime, and days off from separate services. They looked similar in the calendar, but their date handling and visibility rules were not interchangeable.

A day off that moves to yesterday

Take a day-off record with the value 2026-10-23. Parsing that string as midnight UTC and displaying it in Los Angeles can produce October 22. The browser has converted an instant correctly; the mistake is that a day off was never meant to be an instant.

Input Incorrect interpretation Expected result
2026-10-23 — date-only day off Oct 22 — UTC midnight formatted in Los Angeles Oct 23 — preserve the intended calendar day

A shift timestamp is different: it represents a moment that may be displayed at different local times. We kept those two paths separate. Here's a reduced TypeScript illustration of that boundary:

TypeScript · illustrative example (not production code)

type CalendarRecord =
  | { kind: "dayOff"; date: string }
  | { kind: "shift"; startsAt: string };

function toCalendarEvent(record: CalendarRecord) {
  if (record.kind === "dayOff") {
    // Keep the calendar date as a date, not a UTC timestamp.
    return { kind: "dayOff", calendarDate: record.date };
  }

  // A timestamp represents an instant; localize at display time.
  return { kind: "shift", startsAt: record.startsAt };
}

The important choice is that the date-only branch does not call new Date() or silently apply timezone conversion. In a real application, the downstream rendering adapter also needs to preserve that meaning. I would test the same record across timezones and calendar views, not just test the conversion function in isolation.

The boundary before Bryntum

The services weren't returning one shared event format. We could have mapped each response directly into the calendar, then handled the differences in individual views. I chose a typed application event model instead. It gave IDs, categories, date handling, and permission metadata a consistent shape before anything reached Bryntum.

Where service-specific data stops and calendar rendering begins

SERVICE CONTRACTS
  Shifts · overtime           Absences · days off
  Identifiers and time fields Categories and visibility rules
                 ↓
        Typed application event model
        Stable identity · date handling · categories
        Permission metadata
                 ↓
  Product rules               View adapters
  Normalized events           Day · week · month · team
  Consistent access rules
                 ↓
    Bryntum: event layout, interactions, and presentation

The extra mapping layer meant more code and more tests. The alternative was to maintain the same conversion and visibility logic in several places, including day, week, month, and team views. I preferred one boundary where the behavior could be reviewed and tested.

A responsive calendar still needs fresh data

Calendar navigation creates an awkward balance. People move between weeks and return to ranges they recently viewed. Fetching everything again makes the UI feel slow; never refreshing cached results can leave an old schedule on screen.

Example: moving across weeks, then returning

Step Range Action
01 Week 42 Load the visible range
02 Week 43 Navigate forward
03 Week 42 Reuse cached results; revalidate

We reused loaded ranges, debounced quick navigation, and refreshed in the background when needed. The selected date and view could be restored, but the schedule itself still needed revalidation. Another important check was ensuring a late response from an earlier range could not overwrite the one currently on screen.

What I checked beyond the happy path

A populated calendar isn't proof that its data is right. The cases worth checking were the quiet failures: date-only records shifting days, confidential absence details showing in another view, cached ranges not refreshing, and an old request returning after the user had navigated somewhere else.

What I would carry into the next scheduling project is not a particular calendar configuration. It's the decision to make dates, permissions, and data freshness explicit before rendering. That gives the UI library less to guess about, and gives the rest of the application rules that can be tested without opening a calendar.

Originally published on nehamangla.com.Explore more of my engineering work and articles on my portfolio.

articles.title: My Repository Was Haunted. So I Built a CLI -"Exorcist" to Find the Spirits.
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

Exorcist: The Ghosts Hiding in Your Codebase 👻

It is late. You open a repository you have not touched in months.

The feature works. The tests pass. The README looks fine.

Then you notice a configuration file you do not remember adding. A dependency nobody seems to use. A scheduled job whose purpose has been lost to time. Somewhere in the repository, a secret might still be sitting in plain sight.

Nothing is necessarily on fire. That is what makes these things easy to miss.

Software accumulates history. Some of that history is useful; some of it becomes residue: forgotten assumptions, stale code, suspicious configuration, and small risks that survive long after the context behind them disappears.

I wanted to build a tool for investigating that residue without asking developers to hand their source code to a cloud AI service.

That became Exorcist, a local-first command-line tool that scans a repository for selected signals, then uses an open-weight model to help explain what the scanners found.

The idea behind it is simple: the scanners find the evidence; Gemma helps explain it; the developer stays in control.

What I Built

Exorcist is a Python CLI for investigating four kinds of repository “ghosts”:

  • Secrets: potential credentials and sensitive strings that should not be committed.
  • Dependencies: dependency declarations that may deserve a closer look.
  • Dead code: code that appears unused or obsolete.
  • Scheduled jobs: cron or workflow entries that may have been forgotten.

I interpreted the “Ghost in the Machine” theme as the invisible residue software leaves behind. A forgotten token, an obsolete function, or a scheduled task nobody remembers can be easy to overlook precisely because it has become part of the background.

Exorcist turns that investigation into a repeatable workflow:

  1. Scan locally. Run the selected checks against a repository on disk.
  2. Redact sensitive evidence. Mask secret-like values before they are passed into explanations or reports.
  3. Ask Gemma to triage, not to invent evidence. The model classifies and explains scanner findings; it does not replace the scanners.
  4. Validate the response. Pydantic checks structured model output. Exorcist attempts one repair if the output is invalid; if it still fails, the result can be marked for human review.
  5. Generate a report. Produce JSON results or an offline HTML report with findings, verdicts, redacted evidence, model metadata, and scan status.

The CLI includes commands such as doctor, scan, report, guide, rules, tracks, explain, and version. Optional integrations include tools such as Gitleaks and Vulture where appropriate.

I did not want an AI model to confidently declare a repository safe. I wanted a tool that could show its work, explain its conclusions, and be honest when something needs a human.

The first exorcism: a real local demo

For validation, I cloned a small public project, jersey-paglu, and ran Exorcist against the local checkout.

The selected checks completed with zero findings.

That was not a dramatic wall of red warnings, and that is worth saying plainly. A clean result means these selected checks did not detect anything in that run. It does not prove that the repository is universally secure or that every possible issue has been ruled out.

The demo exercised the local model check, plain-text output, JSON output, and HTML report generation. During the scan and report workflow, Exorcist recorded zero network calls. Cloning the repository itself required network access; the scan and report were run against the local copy.

The terminal demo

The generated report

The result I care about is not just the number of findings. It is that the process can be run locally, exported in machine-readable form, and reviewed in a report without requiring a cloud inference call.

Demo

The demo was validated on a local Windows environment using gemma3:4b through Ollama.

# Check that Exorcist and the local model are available
exorcist doctor --model gemma3:4b

# Scan selected categories in a local checkout
exorcist scan ./demo/jersey-paglu \
  --model gemma3:4b \
  --types secrets,deps,deadcode,cron \
  --plain

# Export machine-readable results
exorcist scan ./demo/jersey-paglu \
  --model gemma3:4b \
  --types secrets,deps,deadcode,cron \
  --json

# Generate an offline HTML report
exorcist report ./demo/jersey-paglu \
  --model gemma3:4b \
  --out ./demo/jersey-paglu-real-report.html

Paths may vary by operating system and installation. The target repository must already be available locally before running the offline scan.

The terminal transcript and generated HTML report screenshots above are hosted on DEV.to and show the validation run.

Code

Repository:

ADITYA-KUMAR-2358 / Exorcist

Exorcist

Exorcist is a local-first CLI for finding and banishing possessed code secrets, vulnerable dependencies, dead code, and zombie jobs.

Node CLI

The npm CLI is available as @aditya-kumar-2358/exorcist and provides a Windows Terminal-inspired experience with a cyan EXORCIST wordmark, local Ollama metadata, step-by-step scans, and offline HTML reports.

npx @aditya-kumar-2358/exorcist scan .
npx @aditya-kumar-2358/exorcist scan . --json

The package requires Node 18 or newer. Use --no-color for legacy consoles, --json for automation, and --verbose for diagnostic stack traces.

Sample terminal output

  EEEEE  X   X   OOO   RRRR    CCCC  III  SSS   TTTTT
  E       X X   O   O  R   R  C       I  S       T
  EEEE     X    O   O  RRRR   C       I   SSS    T
  E       X X   O   O  R R    C       I      S   T
  EEEEE  X   X   OOO   R  RR   CCCC  III  SSS    T
  @exorcist/cli  v0.2.0
  Local-first AI code
…
View on GitHub

The most important design decision is the boundary between evidence and interpretation. A scanner can point to a suspicious pattern; the model can help explain why it might matter. But model-generated text should never be accepted as reliable merely because it sounds confident.

A simplified example of the kind of structured contract used to validate triage output looks like this:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal

class FindingTriage(BaseModel):
    verdict: Literal[
        "actionable",
        "needs_review",
        "likely_false_positive",
    ]
    explanation: str = Field(min_length=1)
    confidence: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    recommended_action: str

This is an illustrative example of the validation boundary, not a claim that every internal field or enum is identical to this snippet. The important principle is that model output is parsed and validated before it is used.

The report also needs to be careful about what it repeats. If a tool is investigating a possible secret, it should not create a second place where that secret is exposed. Exorcist redacts sensitive evidence before it is included in explanations and reports.

How I Built It

Exorcist is built with a Python-first stack:

  • Python 3.11+ for the CLI and scanner workflow.
  • Typer for commands and options.
  • Pydantic v2 for validating structured model output.
  • Ollama + Google Gemma 3 4B (gemma3:4b) for local inference.
  • GitPython / Git CLI for working with local repositories.
  • Jinja2 for rendering the HTML report.
  • pytest and Ruff for testing and code-quality checks.
  • Gitleaks and Vulture as optional tools for relevant checks.

The runtime connects to the local Ollama service rather than sending repository content to a hosted LLM endpoint. The model can be selected with --model, which keeps the inference choice flexible instead of permanently coupling the tool to a single model.

The rule: scanners first, AI second

This boundary is the heart of Exorcist:

  • Scanners detect. They produce the evidence a finding is based on.
  • Gemma interprets. It helps classify findings and explain them in language a developer can act on.
  • Pydantic validates. It prevents unstructured model text from being accepted as a reliable result.
  • The developer decides. Ambiguous or invalid output can be flagged for human review instead of being silently treated as fact.

That separation matters. An LLM can produce a plausible explanation for a finding that is wrong, or miss the significance of a real issue. The tool should not confuse fluency with proof.

Exorcist is therefore not a promise that AI can guarantee security. It is a way to make scanner output easier to understand while keeping the evidence and its limitations visible.

Gemma and GitHub Copilot have different jobs

Exorcist uses Google Gemma 3 4B locally through Ollama to classify and explain findings detected by deterministic scanners. This makes the project relevant to Best Use of Gemma: Gemma is part of the product's runtime path, but it is deliberately not the source of truth for detection.

GitHub Copilot was used during development in VS Code to help implement and iterate on CLI features, scanner workflows, reports, documentation, tests, local setup, and demo validation. Copilot is a development assistant; it is not part of Exorcist's runtime product path.

The distinction is important:

Gemma powers the product; Copilot supported the development workflow.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A repository scanner can encounter some of a developer's most sensitive material: source code, configuration, dependency details, and accidentally committed credentials. If every explanation required uploading that material to a closed cloud API, privacy would become a prerequisite problem rather than a design choice.

Open-weight models and local inference change that trade-off.

With Gemma running through Ollama, Exorcist can provide model-assisted explanations without depending on a remote inference service. Developers can inspect the workflow, choose a compatible local model, and adapt the tool to their own repositories and constraints. The scan-and-report path can also work where cloud access is restricted or simply undesirable.

Open innovation matters here for three reasons:

  1. Privacy and control. Source code stays on the developer's machine during the local scan and report workflow.
  2. Adaptability. The model can be changed through a CLI option instead of being hard-wired to a hosted endpoint.
  3. Inspectable boundaries. The project separates deterministic checks from model-generated interpretation, making it easier to reason about what the tool knows and what it is suggesting.

Open-weight does not mean infallible, and local does not mean every result is correct. The scanners have coverage limits, local models can make mistakes, and important findings still deserve human review. The goal is not to remove human judgment. It is to make useful AI assistance more accessible without making cloud inference a requirement.

The Spirit of It

The ghost I wanted to hunt is not supernatural. It is the tiny, forgotten decision that quietly survives in a codebase: a token copied into a config file, a dependency nobody recognizes, or a scheduled task that still runs after its original purpose has disappeared.

These things rarely announce themselves. They hide in ordinary files, between the code a developer actively maintains and the code they no longer remember.

I like the idea of a tool that treats this as an investigation rather than a verdict. It should show what was checked, explain what was found, and admit what remains uncertain. It should not send a repository away to a cloud AI service just to make its output sound more human.

Exorcist does not promise to banish every bug or prove a repository safe. It gives developers a local, explainable starting point: evidence from scanners, a model-assisted interpretation, and a report they can inspect.

For me, the best outcome is not a dramatic red warning. It is a developer understanding what was checked, what was found, what remains uncertain, and what deserves attention next.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Exorcist uses Google Gemma 3 4B locally through Ollama to classify and explain findings detected by deterministic scanners, with zero cloud inference or scan-time network calls.
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: GitHub Copilot was used in VS Code to help build and iterate on the CLI, scanner workflow, reports, documentation, tests, local setup, and demo validation. Copilot is not part of Exorcist's runtime product path.

Built solo, slowly and steadily, by Aditya Kumar.

articles.title: Kernel Bypass Networking: A Deep Dive into Mechanisms, Trade-offs, and the Future
articles.description: The original exploration of kernel bypass networking touched on the essentials: userspace drivers,...
articles.body_html:
The original exploration of kernel bypass networking touched on the essentials: userspace drivers, poll-mode polling, and the loss of kernel safety nets. But a surface-level view misses the fascinating tension in modern systems programming. Why do we keep reinventing the network stack? What exactly are we trading away, and for whom?

This expanded analysis dives into the microarchitectural battlegrounds, the operational realities of cloud-native deployments, and the open research questions that suggest kernel bypass is not a destination, but a spectrum of compromises.

The Core Problem: Why the Kernel Fails at 400 Gbps

To understand the bypass, you must understand the bottleneck. The traditional Linux network stack was designed for generality, not for the extreme packet rates of modern data centers. At 400 Gigabit Ethernet, the packet arrival rate for minimum-sized (64-byte) frames hits approximately 595 million packets per second (Mpps). This leaves a budget of just 1.68 nanoseconds per packet .

The kernel's processing path is dominated by socket buffers (sk_buff), netfilter rule traversals, softirq context switches, and per-core atomic lock contentions. Under these hyper-scale line rates, classical kernel processing "completely collapses," saturating CPU cores at fewer than 15 Mpps per core . Even with optimizations like non-blocking I/O, a single core on a 100 Gbps link might only achieve 20-25 Gbps, requiring 4 to 8 cores just to saturate the link . This inefficiency is the driving force behind every kernel bypass technique.

The Mechanisms: From Brute Force to Surgical Precision

Kernel bypass is not one technology; it is a spectrum ranging from completely evicting the kernel to running safe, programmable code at the earliest possible hook point.

User-Space Drivers (DPDK): The Brute Force Approach

The Data Plane Development Kit (DPDK) represents the classic "full bypass" model. It provides a set of libraries and poll-mode drivers (PMDs) that allow an application to take exclusive control of a NIC queue . The application spins on the hardware ring, eliminating interrupts, context switches, and memory copies.

  • The Win: DPDK delivers the highest raw throughput and lowest latency. In 400G benchmarks, DPDK achieved 542 Mpps across 32 cores, outperforming in-kernel alternatives by roughly 14.8% with 210 ns lower median latency .
  • The Cost: This performance comes at a severe operational price. DPDK burns 100% of a CPU core even at zero traffic (idle polling), consuming over 350W continuously in some configurations . It also completely isolates the NIC from the Linux kernel, breaking standard tools like ethtool, tcpdump, and native container networking .

In-Kernel Fast Paths (eBPF/XDP): The Surgical Strike

The eXpress Data Path (XDP) takes a fundamentally different approach. Instead of leaving the kernel, it runs eBPF bytecode inside the kernel driver, immediately after the packet is received from the hardware ring, before the expensive sk_buff allocation occurs .

  • The Mechanism: An XDP program returns a verdict: XDP_DROP, XDP_PASS, XDP_TX, or XDP_REDIRECT. For bypassing to userspace, the XDP_REDIRECT action can send packets to an AF_XDP socket. AF_XDP is a specialized socket that uses shared memory rings (UMEM) to allow zero-copy packet transfer between the kernel and a userspace application, bypassing the traditional stack while remaining a "first-class citizen" of the kernel .
  • The Win: XDP is not a true bypass; it is an integrated fast path. It preserves kernel routing and security semantics. Benchmarks show it achieves 3.82x higher energy efficiency under variable loads because it can drop into an interrupt-driven mode when idle, eliminating the PMD waste of DPDK . Crucially, it limits L3 cache pollution and DDIO thrashing on co-located applications by 62.4%, making it far friendlier to multi-tenant Kubernetes nodes .

The New Wave: Middleware and Unified APIs

The fragmentation between DPDK, XDP, and RDMA is a major barrier. New research proposes middleware like INSANE, which uses a sidecar architecture to abstract these backends. Developers specify QoS requirements, and the middleware dynamically maps traffic to the best available stack (e.g., DPDK for raw throughput, XDP for integrated filtering) without changing application code .

The Trade-offs: What You Actually Give Up

The JSON iterations repeatedly touched on "trade-offs and pitfalls." The research confirms these are not minor inconveniences; they are fundamental architectural constraints.

1. The Density and Compatibility Wall (The Cloud Killer)
In cloud environments, density is king. Traditional kernel bypass systems are terrible at density. Because they rely on busy-spinning and dedicated cores, you need at least one core per instance. Furthermore, the memory overhead is staggering. Systems like Caladan reserve 648 MB for a single core and scale to only about 200 instances on a 128GB machine. Demikernel uses 167 MB per instance. In contrast, Junction (a newer approach) reduces single-core memory overhead to 29 MB and scales to 3,500 instances .

Compatibility is an even bigger hurdle. Existing bypass systems require applications to be ported. A survey of serverless functions found that Node and Python are among the most popular languages, yet these runtimes have complex OS dependencies that existing bypass systems cannot satisfy. Most state-of-the-art systems support only a handful of C/C++ key-value stores .

2. The Protocol Reality Check
Bypassing the kernel means you often bypass its mature TCP/IP stack. While raw packet processing (L2/L3) is straightforward, implementing a full, correct TCP stack in userspace is "hard" . A 2025 USENIX study compared six kernel-bypass TCP stacks and found that existing stacks cannot handle both bulk data transfers (hundreds of gigabits) and small request-response messages (low latency) simultaneously, or they lack generality . Even for modern protocols like QUIC, which runs in userspace by default, integrating DPDK can yield a 3x speedup (exceeding 10 Gbit/s), but the performance increase is highly implementation-dependent and can sometimes fail to improve at all .

3. The Loss of Operational Sanity
The kernel provides a shared, observable, and secure environment. Bypass shatters this. DPDK requires hugepages, specific NIC firmware, and a debugging workflow that doesn't involve standard sockets . eBPF/XDP, while better, still requires a separate compilation toolchain and verification step. The operational friction is a major reason why these technologies, despite their maturity, remain "hard to integrate into higher-level systems" .

Open Questions and the Path Forward

The exploration of "open questions" reveals that the industry is not converging on a single winner but rather learning to hybridize.

Question 1: How do we make bypass transparent?
The ideal solution is one where unmodified applications automatically benefit from the fast path. Projects like Joyride propose replacing the Linux network stack with a userspace framework that intercepts LibC calls, offering full compatibility without code changes . Junction aims for the same goal with a focus on cloud density, using a shared-memory design to support thousands of instances .

Question 2: How do we balance raw speed with CPU efficiency?
The pure DPDK model of burning cores is unsustainable for general-purpose clouds. The future lies in adaptive models. eBPF/XDP's ability to fall back to the kernel when idle is a step in the right direction . Research into reactive notifications (like the Enso NIC) attempts to solve the busy-polling waste by having the NIC only interrupt the CPU when software signals it is ready to process packets, adapting notification rates to consumption speed .

Question 3: How do we secure the bypass?
When you take the kernel out of the data path, you take away its security guarantees. Userspace drivers and mapped device memory enlarge the trust boundary. The Spectre/Meltdown era demonstrated that hardware isolation is porous. Any bypass framework must now consider how to implement firewalling, connection tracking, and tenant isolation in userspace, or face severe limitations in multi-tenant environments.

The Bottom Line

Kernel bypass networking is not a binary choice between "fast and dangerous" and "slow and safe." It is a design space defined by the specific bottleneck you are trying to eliminate.

  • Choose full userspace bypass (DPDK) when you have a dedicated, latency-obsessed workload (e.g., 5G UPF, market data feed handlers) where the operational cost of burning cores is acceptable, and you are willing to accept complete isolation from the host OS.
  • Choose an integrated fast path (eBPF/XDP/AF_XDP) when you need high performance but must coexist with Kubernetes, standard monitoring tools, and multi-tenant co-location. It offers a "good enough" performance profile with vastly superior operability .
  • Watch the middleware layer as the real enabler. The future of high-performance networking may not be choosing a bypass stack, but rather using a system that chooses the stack for you, dynamically, based on the QoS contract of the moment .

The kernel is not dead; it is being specialized. The art lies in knowing precisely which parts of its workload you can afford to hand over, and to whom.

articles.title: I built a graveyard for dead file formats. Here is how .dbf and .mdb files open in the browser
articles.description: Somewhere in an office right now, a 2009 program is still sending invoices. Nobody has the install...
articles.body_html:
Somewhere in an office right now, a 2009 program is still sending invoices. Nobody has the install disk, the developer retired, and the data lives in a .dbf or an .mdb that nobody remembers how to open.

I work on legacy migrations, so I see this constantly. I wanted a way to say "drop the file here and look at your data" without asking anyone to install anything or upload sensitive company data to a server. So I built a small set of free tools, the File Format Graveyard, and here is how the interesting parts work.

The one rule: the file never leaves the browser

Everything runs client-side. The file goes through file.arrayBuffer() and gets parsed in JavaScript. No upload, no backend, no privacy question, and hosting is a static site. That constraint shaped every decision below.

Reading a .dbf in a few lines

A .dbf (dBase, FoxPro, Clipper) is simpler than it looks. A 32-byte header, then 32-byte field descriptors, then fixed-width records:

const dv = new DataView(buffer);
const records      = dv.getUint32(4, true);  // number of records
const headerLength = dv.getUint16(8, true);
const recordLength = dv.getUint16(10, true);

// Field descriptors: 32 bytes each from offset 32, ending at a 0x0D byte
for (let off = 32; u8[off] !== 0x0d; off += 32) {
  const name   = ascii(u8, off, 11);
  const type   = String.fromCharCode(u8[off + 11]); // C, N, D, L, M...
  const length = u8[off + 16];
}

// Every record starts with a flag byte: 0x2A ('*') means "deleted"
const isDeleted = (i) => u8[headerLength + i * recordLength] === 0x2a;

The format has a few traps, though.

1. Accents are a code page problem. Old DBF files do not use UTF-8. The header declares a code page in byte 29, and TextDecoder does not support the DOS ones (850, 437). The fix is a 128-character table for the upper half of the byte range:

const CP850 = 'ÇüéâäàåçêëèïîìÄÅÉæÆôöòûùÿÖÜø£Ø×ƒáíóúñÑª...'; // 128 chars
const decode = (u8, start, end) => {
  let s = '';
  for (let i = start; i < end; i++) s += u8[i] < 128 ? String.fromCharCode(u8[i]) : CP850[u8[i] - 128];
  return s;
};

Byte 0x82 is é in DOS 850, but a low quotation mark in Windows-1252. Decode "José María" with the wrong one and you get "Jos‚ Mar¡a". So the viewer detects the code page from the header and lets you change it live.

2. Visual FoxPro adds binary types. Integers are plain int32, currency is an int64 divided by 10,000, and datetimes are a Julian day number plus milliseconds since midnight.

3. Deleted records are still in the file, just flagged. The viewer hides them by default.

4. The header can lie. If it declares more records than the file actually holds (a truncated copy, a hand edit), reading blindly gives garbage. I clamp the count with floor((fileSize - headerLength) / recordLength).

5. Memos live in another file. Long text fields point into a .fpt or .dbt file. I do not read those, so they show as (memo) with a warning instead of pretending the data is complete.

Access without Access

For .mdb and .accdb I did not write a parser. mdb-reader (MIT) reads Jet 3/4 and ACE files, including password-protected ones. Two things were needed in the browser:

// Loaded only when someone drops a file, so the rest of the site stays light
const { Buffer } = await import('buffer');
globalThis.Buffer ??= Buffer;
// A dependency written for Node asked for `process`; a tiny shim is enough
globalThis.process ??= { env: {}, browser: true, nextTick: (fn, ...a) => queueMicrotask(() => fn(...a)) };

const { default: MDBReader } = await import('mdb-reader');
const reader = new MDBReader(Buffer.from(arrayBuffer));
reader.getTableNames();
reader.getTable('Customers').getData({ rowOffset: 0, rowLimit: 100 });

The process is not defined error only showed up in the production build, not during my first tests, which is a good reminder to test the bundle you actually ship.

Getting data into Excel

CSV export sounds trivial until Excel opens it. Two details matter: a UTF-8 BOM, so accents survive, and a semicolon separator for locales that use a decimal comma. The export builds a Blob in chunks and yields to the event loop every few thousand rows, so a big table does not freeze the tab. Search works the same way, scanning in chunks of 20,000 rows.

Testing without anyone's real data

I cannot commit customer files, so the DBF tests build synthetic files byte by byte (a dBase III file with deleted records and DOS 850 accents, a Visual FoxPro file with binary types, a truncated file with a lying header). For Access I used the sample databases from the library's own repository. One test failed at first because I had miscalculated the Julian day in the test, not the parser. Writing the expected value by hand is humbling.

Limits

It is read-only. It does not read memo files or indexes, and files over 300 MB are better served by a desktop tool.

Try it, and tell me what is next

  • File Format Graveyard (hub)
  • .dbf viewer
  • Access viewer (.mdb / .accdb)

Which dead format should I tackle next? Paradox? Lotus 1-2-3? Works? If you have a file that nothing will open, tell me what it is.

articles.title: Angular Signal Forms with an Event-Driven NgRx Signal Store
articles.description: Angular 22 landed in June, and the headline in it for me is that Signal Forms are stable. They were...
articles.body_html:
Angular 22 landed in June, and the headline in it for me is that Signal Forms are stable. They were experimental in v21, they are not any more, and they ship with Angular Material and Angular Aria support.

They are worth your attention for 3 things:

  1. The model is a plain signal you own, so the data and the form are never two copies of the same thing drifting apart. Field access is typed off that model: form.title replaces former form.get('title'), and a typo becomes a compile error instead of an undefined at runtime.
  2. Validation lives in a schema, next to the shape it describes, with the error copy on the rule instead of endless template @if chains.
  3. Every piece of form state is a signal, from value and errors to touched, dirty, pending and submitting, so nothing needs subscribing to and ordinary inputs need no ControlValueAccessor anymore.

So it's time to try them out. The form we'll convert belongs to a small task board which features three columns and a form to add a task, backed by a mock API.

The first article put the board's state in a method-based NgRx Signal Store, and the second moved that store to the events plugin, where a component dispatches an event and an effect answers with another one.

The form itself was still built with our good old friend FormBuilder, and in this post we move it to Signal Forms. Most of that is straightforward: fb.group becomes form(), Validators become schema rules, formControlName becomes [formField].

Submitting is the part that isn't, because this form submits to an event-driven NgRx Signal Store, and that's where most of this post goes. Full code is in the repository linked at the end.

The Model Is a Signal You Own

Declaring the Form

A Signal Form starts from data, not from controls. Our task form needs a title, a description and the column the task starts in, so that will be our model: a plain object in a signal, handed to form() together with the rules that define it. Only the title has rules, since it is required and needs three characters:

const EMPTY_DRAFT: NewTask = {
  title: '',
  description: '',
  status: TaskStatus.TODO,
};

readonly draft = signal({ ...EMPTY_DRAFT });

readonly taskForm = form(this.draft, path => {
  required(path.title, { message: 'Title is required' });
  minLength(path.title, 3, { message: 'Title must be at least 3 characters' });
});

With FormBuilder the values used to live inside the FormGroup, and we were only able to reach them through the form. Now they live in a signal we declare ourselves, draft, and form() builds the fields on top of it without taking a copy.

this.draft stays a normal WritableSignal that the rest of our component can read and write. Typing in the bound input writes straight back into it, and setting it updates the input, so there's no patchValue, no form.value, and no moment where the two disagree.

💡 This is the part that changes how a form feels. The model is the source of truth and the form is just a view over it, rather than the form owning a copy that we have to keep syncing.

In the repository the two rules live in one reusable schema() that the form applies with apply(path.title, taskTitleSchema), so a second form, like the board's edit form in the next post, can share it. The inline version above is the same thing, spelled out.

Typed Field Access

taskForm is a field tree shaped like our model. taskForm.title exists because title is on the model, and it's typed as a string field, so if we rename the property the template will stop compiling, which is the part get('title') could never do for us.

Nested models nest too. A { address: { city: string } } model gives us taskForm.address.city, typed all the way down, and applyEach applies a schema to every item of an array field.

Reading Field State

Calling a field, as in taskForm.title(), gives us its state, and every member of that state is a signal:

taskForm.title().value();       // 'Clean the kitchen'
taskForm.title().errors();      // [{ kind: 'minLength', message: '…' }]
taskForm.title().touched();     // false until the user has been near it
taskForm.title().valid();       // and invalid(), dirty(), pending(), required()
taskForm().submitting();        // on the root, while a submit is in flight

value is a writable signal, so taskForm.title().value.set('…') works whenever we need to update a value directly.

💡 Errors are computed whether or not the user has touched the field. An empty required field is invalid from the moment the form exists. touched() is what decides whether we show anything, which matters later when we reset.

Validation in a Schema

The second argument to form() is a schema function. It receives a path tree mirroring our model, and we attach rules to paths, so a rule sits next to the shape it describes rather than in an array on a control constructor.

Built-in Validators

The built-in validators cover the common use cases:

  • required, email, pattern
  • min and max for numbers, minDate and maxDate for dates
  • minLength and maxLength for strings and collections

Each one takes an options object where message is the string our template renders, so the error copy lives with the rule instead of in an @if chain keyed on errors?.['minlength'].

Custom and Async Rules

For any use case the built-in validators don't cover, there is validate, returning an error object or null:

validate(path.title, ({ value }) =>
  value().trim().toLowerCase() === 'untitled'
    ? { kind: 'placeholder', message: 'Give it a real name' }
    : null
);

Async rules get validateAsync and validateHttp, and the field's pending() signal returns true while they run, so a spinner on a username check is a single binding rather than component state we'd have to maintain by hand.

Reusing a Zod Schema

The one I'd use on a bigger form is validateStandardSchema. Signal Forms accept anything implementing Standard Schema, so a Zod or Valibot schema we already maintain for our API types can validate the form too, instead of being restated as form rules:

form(this.draft, path => validateStandardSchema(path, TaskDraftSchema));

Our task board is small enough that the built-ins are the right call, so that stays a pointer rather than something this post demonstrates.

Conditional Rules

Validators aren't the only thing the schema function holds. The same path tree carries conditional logic:

  • disabled, readonly and hidden take a predicate over the model
  • applyWhen scopes a whole block of rules to a condition
  • debounce holds a field's input back from the model, and so from validation, until the user pauses or blurs

So "required only when a checkbox is on" stops being a subscription in ngOnInit.

Binding Fields in the Template

The FormField Directive

One single directive connects a field to a control. Here is the title input of our task form, its error block and the submit button:

<input type="text" [formField]="taskForm.title" class="form-control" />

@if (taskForm.title().touched() && taskForm.title().invalid()) {
  <div class="error-message">
    @for (error of taskForm.title().errors(); track error.kind) {
      <span>{{ error.message }}</span>
    }
  </div>
}

<button type="submit" [disabled]="taskForm().invalid() || taskForm().submitting()">
  @if (taskForm().submitting()) { Adding... } @else { Add Task }
</button>

And here is how it works:

  1. [formField]="taskForm.title" is the whole binding. No formControlName, and no ControlValueAccessor for a standard input.
  2. The error block reads touched() and invalid() together, so nothing shows until the user has been in the field, and then every entry in errors() renders with the message from its rule.
  3. The button's disabled state reads invalid() and submitting() off the root field, instead of a component boolean we'd have to keep in sync.

Custom Controls Without a ControlValueAccessor

[formField] binds a plain <input> with no extra code. A custom component of our own is a different story, and our form has one: the status in the model is picked with 3 buttons, one per column, since until now every new task had to start in To Do.

With reactive forms that picker would implement ControlValueAccessor. With Signal Forms it implements FormValueControl<T> instead, and that contract is much smaller: the only required member is a model() called value.

@Component({ selector: 'app-status-picker', /* … */ })
export class StatusPickerComponent implements FormValueControl<TaskStatus> {
  readonly value = model(TaskStatus.TODO);
  readonly disabled = input(false);
  readonly touch = output<void>();

  readonly options = [
    { status: TaskStatus.TODO, label: 'To Do' },
    { status: TaskStatus.IN_PROGRESS, label: 'In Progress' },
    { status: TaskStatus.DONE, label: 'Done' },
  ];
}

The template is a row of buttons that reads and writes value:

<div role="group" aria-label="Starting column" (focusout)="touch.emit()">
  @for (option of options; track option.status) {
    <button
      type="button"
      [attr.aria-pressed]="value() === option.status"
      [disabled]="disabled()"
      (click)="value.set(option.status)">
      {{ option.label }}
    </button>
  }
</div>

And the task form binds it exactly like the input above:

<app-status-picker [formField]="taskForm.status" />

What each member does:

  1. value is two-way bound to taskForm.status. A click calls value.set(), which writes into draft, and resetting the form to the empty draft moves the pressed button back to To Do.
  2. disabled is optional. Because we declared it, a disabled rule on the status field greys the buttons out with no extra binding.
  3. touch is optional too. Emitting it marks the field touched, and ours emits when focus leaves the group, the same moment a native input would.

Everything beyond value is optional. Anything we do declare is kept in sync with the field's state for us: errors, disabled, readonly, hidden, invalid, pending, touched, dirty, required, and the constraint values min, max, minLength, maxLength and pattern. Checkboxes implement FormCheckboxControl instead, which swaps value for checked.

💡 This is the part to check thoroughly before migrating a design system. A component library only works with Signal Forms once it implements this contract, and a ControlValueAccessor written for reactive forms does not carry over.

What Replaces ngSubmit

One thing to know when we drop ReactiveFormsModule: (ngSubmit) goes with it, so we have 2 options.

  • Handle (submit) ourselves and call preventDefault()
  • Pass submission options into form() and use <form [formRoot]="taskForm">, which hosts novalidate and calls preventDefault() for us

The examples below take the first route, since it keeps the submit logic in the component where it's easier to read.

The Form This Replaced

For contrast, here is what our task board had, and what the 2 previous articles have shown:

taskForm: FormGroup = this.fb.group({
  title: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.minLength(3)]],
  description: [''],
});

createTask() {
  if (this.taskForm.invalid) return;

  this.dispatch.taskCreated({
    title: this.taskForm.get('title')?.value,
    description: this.taskForm.get('description')?.value,
    status: TaskStatus.TODO,
  });
  this.taskForm.reset();
}

It works, but it has no idea whether the task was created. dispatch returns nothing, so the method ends, the form clears, and a failed API call reaches the user as a line in the console.

Signal Forms have an answer for that, and it's where the conversion stopped being a straight swap.

Submitting, and What It Expects of You

The submit() Contract

submit() takes the form and an action it can await. Errors the action returns get routed onto the fields we name:

await submit(this.taskForm, async f => {
  const result = await saveTask(f().value());
  if (result.ok) return;
  return { kind: 'taken', message: 'That title is taken', fieldTree: f.title };
});

It does 3 more things for us:

  • Marks the whole tree touched, so every outstanding error becomes visible at once
  • Refuses a second submit while one is in flight
  • Drives submitting() throughout, which is what the button binding above reads

For a component that calls an HTTP service directly, that's the whole story, and it's a real improvement on wiring those states by hand.

Where an Event-Driven Store Breaks the Assumption

submit() assumes submitting is a function that eventually resolves.

In my previous article our task board moved to the NgRx Signal Store events plugin, where a component never calls a store method. It dispatches an event, a reducer updates state, and an effect performs the side effect and dispatches another event with the result.

That's where submit() gets stuck. dispatch.taskCreated(...) returns void, and the outcome turns up later, elsewhere, as taskCreatedSuccess or taskCreatedFailure. There's nothing to await.

When Binding Is Enough

Not every form needs to await, though. If the template binds to the store's loading and error state, the button can disable itself and an alert can show the failure, and the component never awaits anything. For a lot of forms that is enough, and submit() isn't needed.

Our form wants more than that. It wants submitting() to drive the button, and it wants a duplicate title to land under the title input instead of in an alert at the top of the board. Both of those come from submit(), so the form needs something it can await.

To my knowledge, neither Angular nor NgRx ships a helper that turns an event round trip into a promise. When someone asked for an rxjs-flavoured submit in angular/angular#65199, Angular declined, since the existing RxJS APIs already cover it. On the NgRx side, the answers so far point at the store:

  • In ngrx/platform#5053, the recommendation for Signal Forms with a SignalStore is that the form calls a store method on submit
  • In ngrx/platform#4980, which asks for a promise from rxMethod, the maintainer's answer is a regular method that returns a promise
  • Full-Cycle Reactivity in Angular shows that method being a mutation from @ngrx-toolkit/core

That sounds like the opposite of how an event-driven store works, since components there dispatch events instead of calling methods. It doesn't have to be, as long as the method keeps one rule.

A Mutation That Speaks Events

The rule worth keeping is that the reducer is the only thing that changes tasks. A mutation can keep that rule, as long as it reports its outcome as the same API events the effect used to.

The Mutation

The taskCreated page event and the createTask$ effect that answered it in the previous article are gone. In their place our store gets a createTask mutation:

withMutations(store => ({
  createTask: rxMutation<NewTask, Task>({
    operation: (draft: NewTask) => store._taskService.createTask(draft),
    onSuccess: task =>
      store._dispatcher.dispatch(taskApiEvents.taskCreatedSuccess(task)),
    onError: error =>
      store._dispatcher.dispatch(
        taskApiEvents.taskCreatedFailure(errorMessage(error))
      ),
  }),
})),

Step by step:

  1. operation calls the service with the draft, status included, so the column picked in the form is the column the task lands in.
  2. onSuccess and onError dispatch taskCreatedSuccess and taskCreatedFailure, so the existing reducer adds the task unchanged, and every result still shows up as an event.
  3. Calling store.createTask(draft) returns a promise of { status: 'success' | 'error' | 'aborted' }, which is the thing submit() was missing.

errorMessage is a two-line helper that pulls the message out of whatever the service rejected with and falls back to String(error). Both the mutation and the component use it, so the text under the field is the text the server sent.

_taskService and _dispatcher are props the store injects with withProps: our task service, and the events plugin's Dispatcher from @ngrx/signals/events.

The Component

Now submit() has something to await:

async createTask(event: Event) {
  event.preventDefault();

  await submit(this.taskForm, async f => {
    const result = await this.store.createTask(f().value());

    if (result.status === 'error') {
      return {
        kind: 'server',
        message: errorMessage(result.error),
        fieldTree: f.title,
      };
    }

    this.taskForm().reset({ ...EMPTY_DRAFT });
    return undefined;
  });
}

We await the mutation, turn an error into a message with fieldTree: f.title, and reset on success. A rejected create now lands on the title field as a message under the input, the same way a minLength failure does.

Resetting Without the Error Flashing Back

Writing an empty draft into this.draft clears the form, but "Title is required" appears the instant it does.

The field is still touched, and an empty touched title is required again.

So we use taskForm().reset(value) instead, which clears touched and dirty along with the value.

When I replaced reset() with a plain signal write, no test failed, so the suite now has one that checks touched() is cleared after a successful create.

The Rollback That Was Already There

The mutation only replaced the create path, so everything else our store did in the previous article still works, including the rollback when moving a card fails.

Moving a task between columns is an optimistic update. The reducer applies the change the moment the page event arrives:

on(taskPageEvents.taskStatusChanged, event =>
  updateEntity(
    { id: event.payload.id, changes: { status: event.payload.status } },
    { collection: 'task' }
  )
),

and reverts it when the API disagrees, using the previous status the component sent with the event, and says why in the board's alert:

on(taskApiEvents.taskStatusChangedFailure, event => [
  updateEntity(
    { id: event.payload.id, changes: { status: event.payload.previousStatus } },
    { collection: 'task' }
  ),
  { error: event.payload.error },
]),

The mock fails every status change on task ID 3, so we can watch a card move and snap back. The form now reports its own failures the same way the board does, on a field instead of a column.

💡 Events still run the board. Loading, moving a card and deleting still dispatch events, because nothing awaits them. If a form needs the outcome, it calls a mutation; if nothing waits, dispatch an event.

Testing It

To get a failure only the server can know about, the mock now rejects a duplicate title. This test checks that a server rejection ends up on the title field:

it('routes a server rejection onto the title field', async () => {
  const existing = 'Clean the kitchen'; // seeded in HOUSEHOLD_TASKS
  component.draft.set({ title: existing, description: '', status: TaskStatus.TODO });

  await component.createTask(new Event('submit'));

  const errors = component.taskForm.title().errors();
  expect(errors.map(e => e.kind)).toContain('server');
  expect(errors.map(e => e.message)).toContain('A task with this title already exists');
});

The test seeds the model straight through draft, submits the way the template would, and asserts on the title field's errors() rather than on anything the store exposes. It never touches the mutation directly, so it would pass unchanged against any other way of reaching the server.

Rejecting duplicates broke an existing test, which created the same task twice to prove ids are unique, so it now creates 2 differently named tasks.

When to Reach for Signal Forms

Both form systems live in the same app. @angular/forms and @angular/forms/signals are separate entry points, so this is a per-form decision rather than a migration you have to finish.

Use Signal Forms when:

  • You are on v22 and writing a new form, especially in a component that is already signal-based
  • The form edits data you already have a type for, like a Task, so a renamed or mistyped field fails at compile time instead of in the browser
  • You want a server error, like a duplicate title, to show under the field it belongs to without wiring that up by hand
  • You already keep a Zod or Valibot schema for the same shape and would rather validate against it once

Stick with reactive forms when:

  • You are below v22, where the API was still experimental and moved between releases
  • You have a large body of existing forms, because there is no migration schematic and each one is a manual rewrite
  • You depend on third-party form controls that have not implemented FormValueControl yet
  • The form is a throwaway with one field and no validation, where either option is fine and the familiar one is cheaper

And if the form submits into an event-driven store, give the store a mutation that dispatches its existing events.

💡 I would not go back and convert working forms for the sake of it. The case for Signal Forms is strongest where a form has real validation and a real submit, because that is where the typed schema and the field-level error routing earn their keep. A 3-field contact form is not where you will notice the difference.

  • NgRx custom store features: Known TypeScript Issues, if signalStore() fails with No overload matches this call once a feature declares the state it needs. The fix is an unused generic on the feature, and the signals config of @ngrx/eslint-plugin flags any feature missing it.
  • Previous article: Event-Driven State Management with NgRx Signal Store (the events plugin this post submits into)
  • First article: Using NgRx Signal Store (the method-based store the board started with)

How are you handling submit in a signal-based app? If you've kept a store purely event-driven and found a cleaner way to await the outcome than a mutation, I would like to see it.

articles.title: I built a Perler bead pattern generator that exports your work as a single HTML file
articles.description: If you've never heard of Perler beads (fuse beads): you place tiny plastic beads on a pegged board,...
articles.body_html:
If you've never heard of Perler beads (fuse beads): you place tiny plastic beads on a pegged board, iron them, and they melt into pixel art you can keep. It's physical pixel art — and people make genuinely impressive stuff with it.

Planning a big project requires a pattern: a grid telling you which bead color goes in which cell. Existing online generators do the quantization for you, but I wanted one with a specific superpower: the whole tool, plus your current work, exportable as ONE self-contained HTML file you can keep, email, or open years later.

So I built Perler Bead Blueprint Maker — 100% client-side, no account, no backend, images never leave your browser. Source is on GitHub (MIT).

This post is about how it works and the one bug that taught me to never regex-replace HTML again.

TL;DR — what it does

  • Upload an image → quantized to real bead palettes (Perler, MARD, ARTKAL, YANT — including their actual color codes and names)
  • Preset sizes (29/38/49/69/104…) or any custom N×N
  • Color budget: k-means clustering in Lab space to hit "≤ 25 colors" without visual mush
  • Interactive 2D grid (bead codes printed in cells, highlight tracking, "done" marks that persist)
  • 3D board view with real perler beads (Three.js InstancedMesh) and a depth-layering mode that stacks the board into relief layers
  • Editing tools: brush / fill / eraser / eyedropper with undo history
  • Export: poster PNG/PDF, multi-size PDF collection + CSV shopping list, and — the reason this project exists — a single HTML file that IS the app WITH your work inside

The quantization: Lab space + seeded k-means

Naive RGB distance quantizes badly (blues and purples especially). Everything runs in CIELAB and uses ΔE76 for matching:

// rgb → Lab, then nearest palette color by ΔE76
function nearest(hex: string, palette: Color[]): Color {
  const [L, a, b] = rgb2lab(hex);
  let best = palette[0], bestD = Infinity;
  for (const c of palette) {
    const d = deltaE76(L, a, b, c.lab);
    if (d < bestD) { bestD = d; best = c; }
  }
  return best;
}

For the color budget, a palette of 221 colors reduced to "25 colors max" is a clustering problem. k-means++ in Lab space works well, with one addition: a fixed seed, so the same image always quantizes to the same pattern. Sounds obvious, but most generators re-roll the dice on every page load — you refresh and your carefully-tuned 20-color selection becomes 23 different colors.

The 3D board

Beads are InstancedMesh cylinders — one draw call for thousands of beads — with a canvas-generated texture that fakes the hole. The pegboard underneath has bumps. Nothing fancy, but it sells the illusion:

const geo = new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.42, 0.42, 0.32, 24);
const mesh = new THREE.InstancedMesh(geo, mat, count);
// one setMatrixAt per bead, y offset = board layer

The depth-layering mode is my favorite: a heuristic (brightness + center weighting + smoothing, then equal-frequency bucketing into 7 layers) turns a flat pattern into stacked relief layers — for making actual 3D bead sculptures, shakelight-style.

The single-file export (and the bug that broke it)

The exported file is the entire app bundle + your current state (blueprint, progress, source image as a compressed data URL) embedded in a <script type="application/json"> tag. On open, the app checks that tag, restores state into localStorage, and you continue where you left off. No server, no database — the file is the database.

My first implementation did the injection with a regex:

// ❌ DO NOT DO THIS
html = html.replace(
  /<script id="perlerSaved"[^>]*>[\s\S]*?<\/script>/,
  `<script id="perlerSaved">${json}</script>`
);

It worked… until it didn't. The check I skipped: the marker string perlerSaved also exists inside the bundled JS — in the very restore code that reads the tag, and inside minified variable-containing chunks. The regex matched there first, and replaced ~84KB of application code with a JSON blob. The exported file opened to a white screen.

Two lessons, now burned into the project's docs:

// ✅ DOM-based injection: the parser finds THE element, not any text occurrence
const tpl = document.createElement('div');
tpl.innerHTML = html;
const tag = tpl.querySelector('#perlerSaved');
tag.textContent = json;          // textContent never executes, never mis-matches
html = '<!DOCTYPE html>' + tpl.innerHTML;
  1. Never regex-replace structured markup. Parse, query, mutate, serialize. The regex version produced a file that worked exactly once — when I tested it before the bundle contained the string, and never again.
  2. Test the export against the real production bundle, not a dev build. Dev bundles don't contain minified code that collides with your markers.

Bonus property of this design: the exported file strips external <script src> tags, so your exported copy has no analytics, no external requests — it works offline forever.

Small things that mattered more than expected

  • Printing bead codes inside grid cells came from a single user comment ("no way to know which color goes where without cross-checking the list"). Cells auto-hide codes below ~13px, and text color flips black/white by cell luminance with a contrast outline.
  • Language toggle (中文/EN) — first-use detection from navigator.language, persisted choice. A pixel-art tool is visual, but "MARD 221" labels and toasts still need to be readable.
  • Pointer Events everywhere — one code path for mouse and touch, pinch-zoom included. Writing mouse + touch handlers separately in 2026 is self-harm.
  • Privacy-friendly analytics: GoatCounter, no cookies, event names like e/upload/104/mard48/zh/m (event/size/palette/language/device). One gotcha I hit the hard way: GoatCounter silently classifies traffic from cloud-provider IP ranges as bots — if you test your own site through a VPN/proxy, your dashboard stays at zero and nothing tells you why.

Try it

  • Live: https://perler.phtbyte.com/
  • Source: https://github.com/pht1991/perler-blueprint

Everything runs locally; upload an image, hit the 3D view, and export a single file as a souvenir.

If you build something with a pattern from it (or find a quantization case where it picks a clearly wrong color), I'd genuinely like to hear about it in the comments.

articles.title: No Human Will Ever Write Code Better Than LLMs? Better at What?
articles.description: A tweet went around saying: "No human will ever write code better than LLMs. Accept this fact, stop...
articles.body_html:
A tweet went around saying: "No human will ever write code better than LLMs. Accept this fact, stop pretending, and move on."

Here is my reply.

That's a lot of implicit "better" in that question. LLMs are trained to be plausible, not right. You can get as elegant/idiomatic/smooth-sounding as you want, and still miss the real constraints that matter (existing systems, team patterns, business considerations, failure modes, not-yet-real features).

Senior-level engineering is not just about "writing" code. It's knowing when not to. It's about recognizing real edge cases and not-baked-yet abstractions, knowing when a problem could be more simply solved, or not solved at all. That kind of judgment is hard to quantify, hard to prompt, and often non-obvious in a generated solution.

So yes, LLMs can be a handy tool, but not even close to the level of a real human expert.

The word that bothers me most in that tweet is "better". So I wrote down what it means.

"Better" is a word that we treat like a scalar value. In other words, there is one value that defines better. However, when you ask "better" at what are you measuring it? Lines per minute? Correctness? Maintainability? The courage to not build it? You quickly realize "better" means different things depending on the dimension you are measuring it along.

The productivity metric is lines per minute. It's a nice, simple metric, and it's easy to measure. There's a lot of momentum in this metric because it feels like improvement. However, it is only a measure of typing. It doesn't mean the resulting program is better.

A thousand lines of wrong code is worse than no code at all. A thousand lines of code that crumbles the second you look at it are even worse than that. So, instead we look at correctness. We want our code to be better because it's correct. It has the correct functionality, and it meets the spec. It passes the test. This is an improvement. But, that's not enough.

The real nightmare is that the LLM-generated code works until it doesn't, and it doesn't make sense to you. You'll get reasonable-looking code that somehow finds its way to production, and your payment pipeline will suddenly start silently discarding transactions because the model just decided to add a retry_on_timeout decorator to your transaction handler function that will catch the exception, log a WARNING, and return None. The code down the line will take the None and read it as a zero-dollar successful charge, so now your customers are getting the things they ordered for free.

Gramli tested a case like this in To Retry or Not to Retry. In one scenario, a payment request returned a 503 with a Retry-After header and no idempotency key. Most of the 8 models followed the header and said to retry. Only two said no.

Dex from HumanLayer explains why this happens in his talk "Harness Engineering Is Not Enough and Why Software Factories Fail". Many coding benchmarks give the model a pass or fail reward. The model wins when the tests pass, and nothing penalizes it for bad design. So it learns to add a try/catch or a type cast, because those make the test pass.

We can have a perfectly good piece of software that's unchangeable. This is the opposite of what we want. This is legacy code, and it is bad. We need to be able to make changes without pain.

So we improve it by making it maintainable. Maintainable code is readable, simple code, it's code that doesn't make anyone else want to burn down the office. It doesn't break as time goes on. Maintainable software just works. It meets new requirements and changes without breaking.

The last option is the best of all. It's the metric of wisdom. The "better" that allows us to say "no we shouldn't do that". It's better because it's less, but necessary.

In other words, code is a liability, it is something that we should keep at a minimum. This "better" is the most difficult to practice. It requires saying no to pressure, to budget, to a stakeholder who thinks they have a great idea. It is a less is more metric. However, the compounding interest it pays by not building something keeps growing.

So, "better" is not one thing. It's multiple things. It's a hierarchy, and it changes as we gain experience. We go from lines per minute to correctness to maintainability to not building.

articles.title: How I finally understood the Dependency Inversion Principle
articles.description: The Intro   Last stop. We made it to the D: the Dependency Inversion Principle.  This one is...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Last stop. We made it to the D: the Dependency Inversion Principle.

This one is special because the other four kind of lead here. SRP gave us small classes. OCP taught us to add instead of edit. LSP and ISP gave us honest, tiny interfaces. DIP is where we decide who points at whom.

Buckle up, it's the one that changes how your main.ts looks forever.

The What

The definition has two parts:

High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.

Abstractions should not depend on details. Details should depend on abstractions.

Four sentences that use "depend" five times. Cool cool cool.

Plain version: your business logic should not import your database driver. The important stuff (orders, invoices, rules) should sit at the top and know nothing about the plumbing (Postgres, Stripe, the file system). The plumbing should plug into the business logic, not the other way around.

Let's build an order checkout and watch the arrows flip.

The How

Here is OrderService, the "high-level" part of our store. It's the thing that knows what placing an order means:

// src/order-service.ts
import { PostgresOrderRepository } from './postgres-order-repository.js'
import { StripeClient } from './stripe-client.js'

export class OrderService {
  private readonly orders = new PostgresOrderRepository('postgres://localhost/shop')
  private readonly stripe = new StripeClient(process.env.STRIPE_KEY!)

  async placeOrder(customerId: string, total: number) {
    await this.stripe.charge(customerId, total)
    const id = await this.orders.insert({ customerId, total })
    console.log(`🧾 order ${id} placed`)
    return id
  }
}

The two "low-level" pieces:

// src/postgres-order-repository.ts
export class PostgresOrderRepository {
  constructor(private readonly url: string) {}

  async insert(order: { customerId: string; total: number }) {
    console.log(`🐘 INSERT INTO orders ... (${this.url})`)
    return 'ord_123'
  }
}

// src/stripe-client.ts
export class StripeClient {
  constructor(private readonly apiKey: string) {}

  async charge(customerId: string, amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 stripe charged ${customerId} $${amount}`)
  }
}

And main:

// src/main.ts
import { OrderService } from './order-service.js'

await new OrderService().placeOrder('cus_42', 99)

Run it, it works, everyone goes home. 🏠

Now draw the arrows. Who imports whom?

OrderService  ──▶  PostgresOrderRepository
OrderService  ──▶  StripeClient

The most important class in the app depends on the two most replaceable classes in the app. That's upside down. And here's how you feel it:

  • Want to write a test for placeOrder()? Congratulations, your test now needs a running Postgres and a Stripe API key. For a function with two lines of logic.
  • Marketing wants a free-trial checkout with no payment? You're going to put an if inside OrderService to skip Stripe. Then another for the sandbox. Then...
  • The database team migrates to MySQL? Open OrderService, the one file that should never care.
  • Running it locally charges a real card if STRIPE_KEY is a real key. Ask me how I know. 😬

The service news its own dependencies, so it is welded to them. Let's cut the welds.

Step 1: the high-level module describes what it needs

OrderService needs two things: somewhere to put orders, and something that can take money. It should describe those in its own words, not in Postgres or Stripe words:

// src/order-service.ts
export interface NewOrder {
  customerId: string
  total: number
}

export interface OrderRepository {
  insert(order: NewOrder): Promise<string>
}

export interface PaymentGateway {
  charge(customerId: string, amount: number): Promise<void>
}

export class OrderService {
  constructor(
    private readonly orders: OrderRepository,
    private readonly payments: PaymentGateway,
  ) {}

  async placeOrder(customerId: string, total: number) {
    await this.payments.charge(customerId, total)
    const id = await this.orders.insert({ customerId, total })
    console.log(`🧾 order ${id} placed`)
    return id
  }
}

Two things to notice:

  1. The interfaces live next to the service, because the service owns them. It says "this is what I need". That's the "abstractions belong to the high level" part.
  2. The dependencies come in through the constructor. The service doesn't build them anymore. That's the "dependency injection" part, which is the everyday tool we use to follow DIP.

Step 2: the details plug in 

// src/postgres-order-repository.ts
import type { OrderRepository, NewOrder } from './order-service.js'

export class PostgresOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
  constructor(private readonly url: string) {}

  async insert(order: NewOrder) {
    console.log(`🐘 INSERT INTO orders ... (${this.url})`)
    return 'ord_123'
  }
}

// src/stripe-payment-gateway.ts
import type { PaymentGateway } from './order-service.js'

export class StripePaymentGateway implements PaymentGateway {
  constructor(private readonly apiKey: string) {}

  async charge(customerId: string, amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 stripe charged ${customerId} $${amount}`)
  }
}

Look at the imports now. The Postgres class imports from order-service.ts. The arrow flipped:

PostgresOrderRepository  ──▶  OrderRepository (owned by OrderService)
StripePaymentGateway     ──▶  PaymentGateway  (owned by OrderService)

The plumbing points at the business logic. That's the "inversion".

Step 3: main.ts becomes the only place that knows everything 

// src/main.ts
import { OrderService } from './order-service.js'
import { PostgresOrderRepository } from './postgres-order-repository.js'
import { StripePaymentGateway } from './stripe-payment-gateway.js'

const service = new OrderService(
  new PostgresOrderRepository('postgres://localhost/shop'),
  new StripePaymentGateway(process.env.STRIPE_KEY!),
)

await service.placeOrder('cus_42', 99)

Same output as before. But now the big one: let's write that test.

Step 4: the test that used to be impossible 

// src/order-service.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest'
import { OrderService, type OrderRepository, type PaymentGateway } from './order-service.js'

class InMemoryOrders implements OrderRepository {
  saved: unknown[] = []
  async insert(order: unknown) {
    this.saved.push(order)
    return 'ord_test'
  }
}

class FakePayments implements PaymentGateway {
  charged: number[] = []
  async charge(_customerId: string, amount: number) {
    this.charged.push(amount)
  }
}

test('placing an order charges and saves it', async () => {
  const orders = new InMemoryOrders()
  const payments = new FakePayments()
  const service = new OrderService(orders, payments)

  const id = await service.placeOrder('cus_42', 99)

  expect(id).toBe('ord_test')
  expect(payments.charged).toEqual([99])
  expect(orders.saved).toHaveLength(1)
})

No Postgres. No Stripe. No mocking library. Two tiny classes that implement the interfaces OrderService asked for, and a test that runs in a millisecond.

And the free-trial checkout from earlier? new OrderService(repo, new NoChargeGateway()). Zero ifs inside the service.

The Why

Let's land this plane:

  • Business logic is the stable part; vendors are the volatile part. Stable code should never import volatile code. DIP is just that sentence turned into a rule.
  • Interfaces belong to the consumer. OrderService wrote PaymentGateway in its own vocabulary. Stripe adapted to it, not the other way around. When you swap Stripe for something else, the interface doesn't move.
  • Construction happens at the edge. main.ts (or your DI container, or your framework's wiring) is the only place that says new PostgresOrderRepository(...). Everything inside is handed what it needs.
  • Testing is a side effect, not a goal. We didn't "design for testability". We pointed the arrows the right way and the tests became easy on their own.

If you read my loosely coupled modules post, this should feel familiar. Same move, now with a name and a letter.

The Goodbye

And that's SOLID, all five letters, five tiny projects, five things we broke on purpose. If I had to compress the series into one line:

Small honest pieces, pointed at abstractions, glued together at the front door.

Thanks for riding along. Now go find a new keyword inside a service class and ask it why it's there. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: A Message From Our Founder: On the Winding Down of LaaSy™
articles.description: It is with a heavy heart, and a considerably heavier wool inventory, that I announce LaaSy™ will...
articles.body_html:
It is with a heavy heart, and a considerably heavier wool inventory, that I announce LaaSy™ will cease operations effective immediately.

This is not the outcome we envisioned when we set out to democratize autonomous camelid infrastructure. We believed enterprises were ready for pasture-native computing. We believed the world needed Deterministic Spitting™. We believed, perhaps most fatally, that the market would recognize the existential risk of Unmanaged Wool Sprawl before it was too late.

We were right about the vision. We were wrong about the timeline.

A Brief Post-Mortem

In the interest of transparency, and at the request of our investors, we want to share an honest account of how we arrived here.

Q1. Strong grazing momentum. The seed round closed oversubscribed. The team expanded to forty-seven full-time shepherds and one part-time goat. Morale was high. The pastures were green.

Q2. Series A closed at eighteen million dollars. WolfGuard AI™ entered beta. Early telemetry was promising, though in retrospect we may have over-indexed on predator observability at the expense of, for example, whether the llamas were happy.

Q3. We shipped Retrieval-Augmented Rumination™ to general availability. Adoption was slower than projected. Several enterprise customers reported that their Autonomous Camelid Agents™ had begun ruminating so deeply that they stopped grazing entirely. We classified this as a feature. The market classified it differently.

Q4. The coyotes got in.

What We Learned

Every company failure contains lessons, and we owe it to the ecosystem to name ours plainly.

We learned that a Camelid Control Plane™ operating across cloud, edge, and pasture-native environments is significantly harder to maintain than it is to put on a slide.

We learned that Deterministic Spitting™ is, at a fundamental and possibly biological level, not deterministic.

We learned that "SOC 2 Grazing Certified" is not a certification that exists, a fact our auditors raised somewhat later in the process than we would have preferred.

And we learned that when you build an elite Coyote Red Team™ to continuously probe your pasture boundaries, the coyotes eventually stop being a red team.

On Our B-TAP Attribution Status

We also want to address recent speculation regarding LaaSy™'s standing with the Bureau of Token Attribution and Provenance.

As part of our commitment to responsible AI infrastructure, LaaSy™ maintained extensive observability across every Autonomous Camelid Agent™, Retrieval-Augmented Rumination™ request, predator detection event, and grazing decision.

This turned out to be expensive.

Following a voluntary review that we were strongly encouraged to consider mandatory, B-TAP determined that LaaSy™ had failed to attribute substantial Context Tax, Retrieval Tax, Prose Tax, and Observer's Tax across its operations.

We respectfully disagree with several aspects of the finding.

In particular, we continue to maintain that sending the complete Herd Knowledge Graph to every llama before each grazing decision was necessary for enterprise-grade contextual awareness. B-TAP has characterized this practice as "reckless context hydration."

Our attorneys have advised us that B-TAP has no ability to compel, fine, or otherwise reach us, and that we should therefore be significantly more relaxed about this than we are.

We can, however, confirm that a significant portion of our unattributed Observer's Tax resulted from telemetry systems installed to determine why our token costs were increasing.

Those telemetry systems increased our token costs.

We subsequently deployed additional agents to observe the telemetry systems.

This did not improve matters.

The finding also identified a substantial amount of Prose Tax associated with internal strategy documents. Management disputes B-TAP's determination that the phrase "pasture-native agentic transformation ecosystem" could have been replaced with "llamas."

LaaSy™ has been entered into the Public Register of Non-Attributed Systems. We are unable to confirm this, because no one has ever been able to open the Public Register of Non-Attributed Systems.

Our appeals agent is currently reviewing the 14,882-page framework and has requested additional context.

We have turned it off.

On the Series C

Many of you have asked about the Series C.

The Series C did not close.

We remain grateful to Sand Hill Pastures Capital, Andreessen Alpacowitz, and Sequoia Grazing Partners for their early belief in us. We understand and respect their decision to reallocate toward opportunities with clearer paths to revenue, stronger unit economics, fewer unresolved attribution findings, and fewer actual animals.

We note, without further comment, that The General Mills Artificial Intelligence Initiative has returned its attention to breakfast cereals.

Migration and Offboarding

We know many of you have workloads still grazing in production, and we are committed to a responsible transition.

Effective today, all herds will be released to open pasture. We recommend customers export their wool, hay, tribal herd knowledge, and spit metadata before the fences come down at end of quarter. Because you maintained complete ownership under our Local-First Camelid Architecture™, this data was always yours. This was, in the end, one of the few promises we kept entirely.

The Herd Knowledge Graph will remain available in read-only mode for ninety days, after which it will be, appropriately, put out to pasture.

A Personal Note

Building LaaSy™ has been the honor of my professional life.
