To our shepherds, our engineers, our one part-time goat: thank you. To our customers who trusted us with their most critical grazing workloads: thank you, and we are sorry. To the coyotes: well played.

We set out to prove that camelid sovereignty mattered. I still believe it does. Perhaps the next company to attempt this will succeed where we could not, ideally with better fencing.

The pasture is quiet now. The wool remains un-sheared. And somewhere, a single part-time goat is updating its résumé.

We were told, at the very beginning, that none of this would be a problem.

No Prob-Llama™.

Information without provenance is just gossip.

Camelids without provenance are just fuzzy rumors.

And a startup without revenue is just a very expensive petting zoo.

articles.title: How UPI Works: The ₹0 Magic Behind Every Scan-and-Pay (System Design)
articles.description: System Design Simplified — Part 1                   The chai stall   It's 8 AM. You're holding a...
articles.body_html:
System Design Simplified — Part 1

The chai stall

It's 8 AM. You're holding a cutting chai in one hand and your phone in the other. You scan a faded QR code on the counter, type four digits, and before Bablu looks up from his kettle, his phone says ₹20 received.

Two seconds. No card. No cash. No fee.

In August 2026 alone, UPI handled a record 24.51 billion transactions, about 791 million a day. That's roughly 85% of India's digital payments and nearly half of all real-time payments on Earth.

So what happened in those two seconds? Let's follow your ₹20.

Meet the cast

Every UPI payment has five characters, and each has exactly one job.

You. The person with the phone.

Your UPI app. PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm. It does not hold your money. It's a messenger.

Your bank. Where your money lives. The only one allowed to take ₹20 out.

NPCI. The National Payments Corporation of India. It runs one central switch that every bank is plugged into. It holds no money either. It's the traffic cop at the junction.

Bablu's bank. Where the ₹20 lands.

One idea to remember: apps and NPCI are messengers. Only banks touch money.

The journey of ₹20, in motion

Purple = the request. Orange = the money. Green = done. Watch it loop once and the whole system makes sense.

Notice the order. Your bank is asked first. Money leaves your account before anyone asks Bablu's bank to accept it. That's deliberate: money stuck in transit can be reversed; money credited that was never debited cannot.

Wait, so what is Google Pay?

This is the part most explainers skip.

Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm, CRED, Amazon Pay are not banks. NPCI has a strict rule: it talks only to banks. So how does an app made by Google reach the switch?

It borrows a bank.

Every UPI app partners with one or more licensed banks, called PSP banks (Payment Service Provider). The bank owns the actual connection to NPCI. It gets audited, holds the security certificates, and takes legal responsibility for every request the app sends. The app, officially a Third-Party Application Provider, rides on the bank's pipe.

You've seen this without noticing. The @okaxis in ramesh@okaxis means Google Pay is using Axis Bank as its PSP. @ybl is PhonePe on Yes Bank. @paytm is Paytm's own handle. The part after @ names the app's partner bank, not yours.

That's the twist: your money can sit in SBI while your Google Pay handle says Axis. Axis is the doorman who walks your request into NPCI. SBI still opens the vault.

Why build it this way? NPCI would rather trust 50 regulated banks than vet 500 apps. If an app misbehaves, its PSP bank answers for it.

There's a real-world reason the big apps now keep several PSP banks. In March 2020, PhonePe ran only on Yes Bank. When RBI put Yes Bank under a moratorium, NPCI blocked its handles, and PhonePe went down with it. Within months PhonePe added ICICI (@ibl) and later Axis (@axl). Today, if one partner bank is slow, the app quietly routes through another.

What NPCI actually does

The switch isn't a black box. It does four jobs on every single payment.

Directory. It keeps the phonebook. bablutea@okaxis maps to a real bank and account number. You never see that mapping, and neither does the person paying you.

Router. It asks your bank to debit first, then asks the receiver's bank to credit, each with a strict timeout. A slow bank gets marked pending; the switch moves on.

Tracker. If a reply never comes back, NPCI doesn't guess. It marks the payment pending, runs a check-status call, and reverses the debit if the credit never landed.

Tally. It records what every bank owes every other bank, all day. More on that below.

NPCI talks only to banks, over private certified lines. It never holds money and never sees your PIN.

The clever ideas inside

Your UPI ID is a nickname. ramesh@okaxis is like a saved contact. NPCI keeps the phonebook. Share it on a poster, switch banks later, the ID stays.

Your PIN never travels. You type it into a locked box provided by NPCI, called the common library. It's encrypted right there on your phone, and only your bank has the key. Google Pay cannot read your PIN. Neither can NPCI. Neither can Axis.

Your phone is the password. During setup, the app sends a silent SMS from your SIM. That binds your number, SIM and device together. There's no username. Your phone is the login; your PIN is the second factor.

It's a switch, not a wallet. A wallet has to hold your money. UPI never does. Money moves bank to bank, so there's no top-up, no middleman, no fee hiding in the spread.

When things go wrong

Money debited, Bablu shrugs, nothing received. What happened?

Your bank said yes and debited you. Then a message got lost between the switch and Bablu's bank. UPI doesn't guess. It marks the payment pending, and NPCI runs a check-status call to learn the truth. If the credit never landed, a reversal goes to your bank and the ₹20 comes back, usually within hours.

The promise: money is never in two places, and never nowhere. It's with you, with them, or in a tracked pending state that will resolve.

Did the banks actually move money?

Here's what almost nobody knows. When your bank debits ₹20 and Bablu's bank credits ₹20, the two banks haven't exchanged a rupee yet. Each just updated its own customer's balance.

Think of two friends who keep paying for each other all week. They don't hand over cash every time; they keep a tally and settle the difference on Sunday. NPCI is the friend with the notebook. Several times a day it tells the Reserve Bank of India "Axis owes SBI ₹340 crore net," and one transfer settles millions of chai payments.

That's why UPI is instant and free at the same time. The expensive part, moving real money between banks, happens only a few times a day, in bulk.

How does one switch survive 791 million hits a day?

Nobody waits for anyone. Every hop has a strict timeout. A slow bank gets marked pending; the switch moves on. Slow banks hurt their own customers, not the country.

The switch is stateless, copied many times. It only routes messages, so dozens of identical copies sit behind a load balancer. Any copy can handle any payment. One dies, nobody notices.

Every message has an ID that can't be reused. If your app resends because the network blinked, the switch sees the same transaction ID and says "already done" instead of charging you twice. This is called idempotency. It's the single most important idea in payments.

Five things to remember

  1. Apps and NPCI are messengers. Only banks hold money.
  2. Google Pay isn't a bank. It reaches NPCI through a partner PSP bank, named by the @ in your UPI ID.
  3. Your PIN is encrypted on your phone; only your bank can read it.
  4. Debit first, credit second. Pending is a tracked state, not a bug.
  5. Banks settle in batches, which is why instant can also be free.

Next in the series

Part 2: How Google Pay handles the Payment Pending screen without losing your money. Retries, timeouts and idempotency, told through one stuck ₹500.

Numbers from NPCI's monthly statistics for August 2026. Bablu Tea Stall is fictional; the system is not.

articles.title: Rust for Gophers, Lesson 3: Structs, Enums, and Match
articles.description: 1. Structs   Rust structs look like Go structs, with three differences that matter: there...
articles.body_html:
1. Structs

Rust structs look like Go structs, with three differences that matter: there are no zero values, there is no embedding, and behaviour like printing or comparing is opted into with derive.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct User {
    name: String,        // owned: the struct owns its data (Lesson 2)
    email: String,
    active: bool,
    login_count: u64,
}

let u = User {
    name: String::from("syam"),
    email: String::from("s@x.dev"),
    active: true,
    login_count: 0,       // every field must be set; no implicit zero values
};

let u2 = User {
    name: String::from("ana"),
    ..u.clone()           // struct update syntax: take the remaining fields from another value
};

No zero values. Go silently fills omitted fields with 0, "" or nil. Rust makes you write every field, so adding a field to a struct turns every construction site into a compile error until you handle it. That's a refactoring safety net. When you do want defaults, opt in:

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct Config {
    port: u16,
    verbose: bool,
    name: String,
}

let c = Config { port: 3000, ..Default::default() };  // the rest is 0 / false / ""

Struct fields are almost always owned types (String, Vec<T>), not references. A struct holding &str needs a lifetime annotation and can't outlive the data it borrows. That's sometimes right (Lesson 8), but owned fields are the default choice.

Tuple structs and the newtype pattern 

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd)]
struct Meters(f64);

let d = Meters(3.0);
let raw = d.0;         // fields are accessed by position

Wrapping a primitive in a one-field struct is called a newtype. It costs nothing at runtime, but Meters and Feet (or UserId and OrderId) become different types the compiler won't mix up. Go's type UserID int64 is similar, but Go converts between them freely with UserID(x). Industry Rust uses newtypes heavily for IDs and validated values.

derive: opting in to behaviour

Derive Gives you Go equivalent
Debug {:?} printing %v / %+v (automatic in Go)
Clone .clone() deep copy Manual copying
Copy Implicit bitwise copy; only if every field is Copy Value semantics for small structs
PartialEq, Eq == and != == on comparable structs
PartialOrd, Ord <, >, sorting No built-in equivalent
Hash Usable as a HashMap key Map keys must be comparable
Default T::default() Zero values

A good habit is to derive Debug on every type, and Clone/PartialEq when they make sense. Copy is only for small, plain-data types; never derive it on something that owns heap memory (the compiler won't let you anyway).

2. impl blocks: methods and constructors

Methods live in an impl block separate from the struct definition, much like Go's func (u *User) ... methods live outside the type declaration. The difference is the receiver: Go has two kinds (value and pointer), Rust has three, and they are exactly the three ownership modes from Lesson 2.

impl User {
    // Associated function (no self): Rust's constructor convention, like Go's NewUser
    fn new(name: &str, email: &str) -> Self {
        Self {
            name: name.to_string(),
            email: email.to_string(),
            active: true,
            login_count: 0,
        }
    }

    fn display_name(&self) -> &str {   // borrows self read-only
        &self.name
    }

    fn record_login(&mut self) {       // borrows self exclusively, may modify
        self.login_count += 1;
    }

    fn into_email(self) -> String {    // takes ownership; u is unusable afterwards
        self.email
    }
}

let mut u = User::new("syam", "s@x.dev");   // :: calls an associated function
u.record_login();                            // . calls a method; &mut u is taken automatically
let email = u.into_email();                  // u is moved here
Receiver Go equivalent Use when
&self func (u User) or func (u *User) that only reads Getters, computations. Most methods
&mut self func (u *User) that writes Changing state
self No equivalent Consuming or converting: into_* methods, builders

Naming conventions you will see everywhere: new for the main constructor, with_* for alternatives (Vec::with_capacity), as_* for cheap borrowed views (as_str), to_* for expensive conversions that allocate (to_string), and into_* for conversions that consume self. Getters are named after the field (name()), never get_name().

Self (capital S) is an alias for the type the impl is for. Use it in constructors and return types so renaming the type later only touches one line.

The method call u.record_login() is sugar for User::record_login(&mut u). Rust auto-borrows the receiver, which is why you never write (&mut u).record_login(). Go does the same thing when it takes &u for pointer-receiver methods.

3. Enums: the feature Go doesn't have

A Rust enum is a sum type: a value that is exactly one of several variants, where each variant can carry its own data. This is the single feature Go programmers miss most once they've used it.

The simple case looks like Go's iota constants:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum Status {
    Active,
    Suspended,
    Deleted,
}

The difference is that Status is a real type. A Go type Status int accepts Status(42), which is a status that doesn't exist. A Rust Status can only ever be one of those three values.

The powerful case is variants with data:

enum Shape {
    Circle { radius: f64 },          // struct-like variant
    Rect { w: f64, h: f64 },
    Triangle(f64, f64, f64),         // tuple-like variant
}

impl Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 {
        match self {
            Shape::Circle { radius } => std::f64::consts::PI * radius * radius,
            Shape::Rect { w, h } => w * h,
            Shape::Triangle(a, b, c) => {
                let s = (a + b + c) / 2.0;
                (s * (s - a) * (s - b) * (s - c)).sqrt()
            }
        }
    }
}

How you would write this in Go:

type Shape interface{ Area() float64 }
type Circle struct{ Radius float64 }
type Rect struct{ W, H float64 }
// ... plus a type switch somewhere:
switch s := shape.(type) {
case Circle: ...
case Rect: ...
// forgot Triangle? compiles fine, silently does nothing
}
Go interface + type switch Rust enum + match
Set of variants Open: anyone can implement the interface Closed: exactly the variants listed
Missing a case Compiles; bug at runtime Compile error
Can be nil Yes No
Memory Usually boxed behind an interface pointer, often a heap allocation Stored inline: size of the largest variant plus a tag

Rust also has the open kind of polymorphism (traits, Lesson 5). Use an enum when you know all the cases (tokens, commands, HTTP methods, states in a state machine, errors). Use a trait when other code needs to add new types. In real Rust code, enums are everywhere: Option, Result, JSON values, AST nodes, and the messages sent between threads.

4. Option<T>: no more nil

Rust has no nil. A value that might be absent has the type Option<T>, which is just an ordinary enum from the standard library:

enum Option<T> {
    Some(T),
    None,
}

The point is that Option<User> and User are different types. You cannot call .name on an Option<User>; you must first handle the None case. So the Go bug "forgot to check for nil, panicked in production" becomes a compile error. And when a function returns plain User, you know for certain it's there.

It also costs nothing: Option<&User> is the same size as &User, because the compiler uses the impossible null address to represent None.

fn find_user<'a>(users: &'a [User], name: &str) -> Option<&'a User> {
    users.iter().find(|u| u.name == name)
}

(The <'a> is needed because there are two reference inputs, as in Drill 5. It says the returned reference borrows from users, not from name.)

Everyday ways to handle an Option 

// 1. match: handle both cases explicitly
match find_user(&users, "ana") {
    Some(u) => println!("found {}", u.email),
    None => println!("not found"),
}

// 2. if let: you only care about the Some case
if let Some(u) = find_user(&users, "ana") {
    println!("found {}", u.email);
}

// 3. let else: unwrap or leave the function early (Go's `if x == nil { return }`)
let Some(u) = find_user(&users, "ana") else {
    return;
};

// 4. Combinators: transform without unwrapping
let name = find_user(&users, "zed")
    .map(|u| u.name.as_str())   // Option<&User> -> Option<&str>
    .unwrap_or("nobody");       // fall back to a default

// 5. The ? operator: inside a function returning Option, return None early
fn first_even(xs: &[i32]) -> Option<i32> {
    let first = xs.first()?;    // if None, return None from first_even right now
    if first % 2 == 0 { Some(*first) } else { None }
}
Method Does Use it when
map(f) Transforms the inner value if Some Chaining a computation
and_then(f) Like map, but f returns an Option itself Chaining steps that can each fail
unwrap_or(v) / unwrap_or_default() Gives the value or a fallback A sensible default exists
unwrap_or_else(f) Fallback computed lazily The fallback is expensive
ok_or(err) Turns Option into Result Lesson 4
is_some() / is_none() Tests without taking the value Only for checks; prefer if let when you'll use the value
copied() / cloned() Option<&T> to Option<T> Getting an owned value out of a lookup
unwrap() / expect("why") Panics on None Tests and genuinely impossible cases only

On unwrap(): in production code, treat it as a red flag. Each one is a potential panic. If you are certain it can't fail, use expect("reason it can't fail") so the panic message explains your assumption. In reviews, I'll ask you to justify each one.

5. Pattern matching in depth

A pattern describes the shape of a value and pulls pieces out of it in one step. Patterns appear in match, if let, let else, while let, let, and function parameters.

enum Command {
    Quit,
    Move { x: i32, y: i32 },
    Say(String),
}

fn run(cmd: &Command) -> String {
    match cmd {
        Command::Quit => "bye".to_string(),
        Command::Move { x: 0, y } => format!("vertical {y}"),        // literal inside a pattern
        Command::Move { x, y } if x == y => format!("diagonal {x}"), // match guard
        Command::Move { x, y } => format!("move {x},{y}"),
        Command::Say(msg) => msg.clone(),
    }
}

Things to notice:

  • Arms are checked top to bottom, and the first match wins. Put specific patterns before general ones. The compiler warns about an arm that can never be reached.
  • Matching on &Command gives references. Because cmd is a reference, msg binds as &String, not String, so nothing is moved out of the borrowed value. This feature is called "default binding modes" and it's why you rarely write & or ref in patterns.
  • Exhaustiveness is your refactoring tool. Add a Command::Jump variant, and every match that doesn't handle it becomes a compile error that lists exactly where to update. Avoid a lazy _ => arm on your own enums, because it switches that check off.

The pattern toolbox 

match age {
    0 => "newborn",
    n @ 1..=12 if n < 3 => "toddler",   // @ binds the value while testing a range
    1..=12 => "child",
    13..=19 => "teen",
    _ => "adult",
}

match point {
    (0, 0) => println!("origin"),
    (x, y) if x == -y => println!("anti-diagonal"),
    (x, _) => println!("x={x}"),           // _ ignores a part
}

let User { name, email, .. } = user;      // destructure a struct; .. ignores the rest

let is_gone = matches!(status, Status::Suspended | Status::Deleted); // bool from a pattern

if let, let else, while let 

if let Command::Say(msg) = &cmd {          // one variant you care about
    println!("{msg}");
}

let Some(expr) = env::args().nth(1) else {  // unwrap or exit: flat code, no nesting
    eprintln!("usage: rpn <expr>");
    process::exit(1);
};

let mut stack = vec![1, 2, 3];
while let Some(top) = stack.pop() {         // loop until the pattern stops matching
    print!("{top} ");                       // 3 2 1
}

let else is the closest thing to Go's guard-clause style (if err != nil { return }). It keeps the happy path unindented, and the else block must leave the scope (return, break, continue, or exit). Industry Rust uses it heavily at the top of functions.

6. Exercise: a stack, and an RPN calculator on top of it

You'll build the stack data structure, then use it to evaluate Reverse Polish Notation, where the operator comes after its operands: 3 4 + 2 * means (3 + 4) * 2. It's a classic stack problem, and it exercises structs, methods, enums with data, match and Option together.

cargo new rpn && cd rpn
cargo run -- "3 4 + 2 *"    # 14
cargo run -- "10 2 -"       # 8
cargo run -- "-3 4 *"       # -12  (a negative number, not the operator)
cargo run -- "1 0 /"        # stderr: error: invalid expression, exit 1
cargo run -- "1 +"          # stderr: error: invalid expression, exit 1
cargo run                   # stderr: usage: rpn "<expression>", exit 1

How RPN evaluation works: read tokens left to right. A number gets pushed. An operator pops two values (the first pop is the right operand), applies itself, and pushes the result. At the end, exactly one value must remain on the stack.

Part A: the stack

  • [ ] struct Stack wrapping a Vec<i64>, with #[derive(Debug, Default)].
  • [ ] Methods with the right receivers: new() -> Self, push(v: i64), pop() -> Option<i64>, peek() -> Option<&i64>, len() -> usize. Choosing &self vs &mut self for each is part of the exercise.
  • [ ] Tests: pop on an empty stack, push then peek, and LIFO order after several pushes.

Part B: the calculator

  • [ ] enum Op { Add, Sub, Mul, Div } and enum Token { Num(i64), Op(Op) }.
  • [ ] fn parse_token(s: &str) -> Option<Token>, written as one match on the string.
  • [ ] A method impl Op { fn apply(self, a: i64, b: i64) -> Option<i64> } that returns None on overflow and on division by zero.
  • [ ] fn eval(expr: &str) -> Option<i64> using your Stack. Use ? so you never write nested matches on pop().
  • [ ] main uses let else for the missing argument and exits with code 1 on any error. No unwrap(), no .clone().
  • [ ] Tests for eval: the examples above, plus empty input, an unknown token like x, and leftover values like "1 2".
  • [ ] cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy -- -D warnings && cargo test pass.

Hints (read only when stuck)

  1. Most Stack methods are one line that forwards to a Vec method. Look at Vec::pop and slice::last in the docs.
  2. In parse_token, a _ => arm can try s.parse::<i64>(). That returns a Result; .ok() turns it into an Option, and .map(Token::Num) wraps the number. Yes, an enum variant can be passed as a function.
  3. Integers have checked_add, checked_sub, checked_mul and checked_div, and each returns an Option. checked_div already handles division by zero.
  4. Op holds no data, so derive Clone, Copy on it. Then apply can take self by value without moving anything important.
  5. Gotcha: in a binary crate, a method nobody calls triggers a dead_code warning, and -D warnings turns that into an error. Use len() and peek() in eval to check that exactly one value remains and to read it. That's their natural job anyway.

articles.title: Why Changing an Agent Harness Breaks Frozen Models
articles.description: Benchmarking coding agent harnesses with a frozen model conflates interface capabilities with policy mismatch.
articles.body_html:
Whenever a team releases a new agent harness, the evaluation script looks the same. You take a popular checkpoint, wire it up to the new prompt templates, tool signatures, and system loop, and measure task resolution against an older setup.

If the success rate drops, the team concludes the new harness is worse.

A new paper from Jian Mu, Ruibo Shen, and Yao Shu at HKUST (Your Policy Is Secretly a Harness: The Decision Geometry of Agent Interfaces, arXiv:2610.37255) shows why this standard comparison is broken. Under KL-regularized control, an optimal policy inherits the structural preferences of the exact harness it was post-trained on. When you evaluate harnesses using a frozen model, you are not testing which harness offers a better ceiling. You are measuring the combination of that ceiling and the mismatch penalty incurred by a policy trained on a different setup.

The paper formalizes deployed return as two distinct terms:

Return = Ceiling(Harness) - Mismatch(Policy, Harness)

The ceiling represents the maximum return possible under that harness. The mismatch represents the return lost because the current model makes suboptimal decisions under those specific interface mechanics.

Weight training moves mismatch. Swapping the harness moves both terms simultaneously.

The sensitivity of frozen policies

When an agent undergoes post-training under a specific harness, its log odds align with that harness's action distribution. The model learns to expect observations in a precise order, predicts tool responses shaped by particular wrappers, and paces its reasoning around a concrete turn loop.

The authors tested this sensitivity on MiniWoB++. They took a trained policy that solved 85.0% of tasks, kept all task semantics identical, and simply reversed the order of the observation fields in the prompt.

Every optimal action remained completely valid and achievable. Yet the success rate of the frozen model collapsed from 85.0% to 19.2%.

If you treated that test as an interface comparison, you would conclude that field order destroyed the environment. In reality, the environment ceiling remained identical, while the policy mismatch exploded because the frozen weights expected the original token layout.

Conversely, the authors found that every harness rejected by a frozen-model comparison that actually raised the theoretical ceiling went on to outperform the original harness once the agent was trained under it. Measuring ceiling and mismatch beforehand accurately predicted those downstream gains.

Measuring coding harnesses on Terminal-Bench Lite

To see how this plays out in production environments, the team evaluated five prominent coding agent setups on Terminal-Bench Lite: DeepAgents, Pi, DeepSeek Harness, Terminus-2, and mini-SWE-agent. They ran a frozen Qwen3.5-9B across all five harnesses and used GPT-5.6 Luna as a teacher stand-in to estimate the true ceiling.

The ranking of actual task accuracy matched the ranking produced by estimating the ceiling minus mismatch:

Harness Ranking on Terminal-Bench Lite:
1. DeepAgents      (High ceiling, controlled mismatch via runtime recovery)
2. Pi              (Interactive terminal steering, compact state representations)
3. DeepSeek Harness (Structured tool profiles, rigid parameter enforcement)
4. Terminus-2      (Tmux session tracking, heavy prompt overhead on small models)
5. mini-SWE-agent  (Minimalist shell loop, lower structural ceiling on complex tasks)

Looking at either metric in isolation failed to predict performance. Looking only at raw accuracy hid whether a harness was genuinely limited or whether Qwen3.5-9B was stumbling over unexpected tool schema definitions.

For instance, Terminus-2 uses tmux keystroke buffers and native summarizer subagents. That architecture offers high ceiling capabilities on long interactive debugging tasks, but imposes high mismatch on smaller local models that fail to track asynchronous terminal state without specific fine-tuning. Meanwhile, mini-SWE-agent has low mismatch because its single-shot bash runner matches standard base model pretraining, but its ceiling is lower when tasks require managing multi-step background processes.

Stop treating harnesses as plug-and-play skins

The immediate takeaway for anyone building agent harnesses is clear: stop benchmarking harness revisions against frozen base checkpoints and calling it an architectural verdict.

When you modify prompt scaffolding, rewrite tool JSON schemas, or change how subagents pass context back to the root, you alter the action space. If your evaluation run shows a 10% regression on a base checkpoint, that regression does not prove your new tool schema is bad. It often means your model spent its post-training budget learning the quirks of your old schema.

If you want to compare harnesses fairly, you have two real options. You either fine-tune checkpoints under each harness candidate to measure adapted return, or you estimate the harness ceiling using a stronger teacher model and evaluate mismatch explicitly.

Anything else is just testing how well a model memorized the flaws of your first prototype.

articles.title: My Daemon Dropped 1,000 Records and Reported Success
articles.description: A soak test came back green. Chain intact, verify-store fine, p99 latency 0.36 ms. Then I counted the...
articles.body_html:
A soak test came back green. Chain intact, verify-store fine, p99 latency 0.36 ms. Then I counted the rows: 9,016 out of 10,000. About a thousand records had gone missing, and every caller had been told the write succeeded.

This is the kind of failure that a background thread holding a lock the hot path needs produces — and raising a buffer to "fix" it is the wrong first move.

Two threads, one lock

The agentwatch recorder daemon — one tool in agentic-suite, a suite of open-source, harness-agnostic security tools for AI agents — has two threads that matter.

Thread 1 — Accept (the hot path): accepts Unix socket connections from hooks, reads the message, normalizes it, appends it to the hash-chained store.

def _append(self, record):
    with self._lock:            # ← needs store._lock
        self.store.append(record)

Thread 2 — Sweeper (background verification): every 5 seconds, reloads the store from disk and re-verifies the entire hash chain. This is continuous verification — if someone tampers with the store file mid-session, the sweeper detects it and flips health to degraded.

def _sweep_loop(self):
    while not self._stop.wait(5.0):
        self.chain_status = self.store.refresh()   # ← the problem

Both threads need store._lock. And refresh() was greedy about it:

def refresh(self):
    with self._lock:
        self._entries = self._load()   # read the ENTIRE file from disk
        self._recount()
        return self.verify()           # recompute EVERY hash — O(n)

Reading the file and rehashing the chain, start to finish, with the lock held the whole time. At small scale this is invisible — and that's exactly why it survives into a soak test.

What that cost

At a thousand entries it's nothing. Eleven milliseconds. At five thousand, fifty-six. At ten thousand, about a hundred and sixteen. By the end of a 10k-send soak the store held around twenty thousand entries, and a single sweep took 242 milliseconds.

Here's what happens during those 242 ms:

  1. The sweeper acquires store._lock.
  2. It reads the entire store file from disk (_load()).
  3. It recomputes every hash in the chain (verify() — O(n)).
  4. Meanwhile, the accept thread tries to append(). It blocks on store._lock.
  5. New hook connections queue in the listen backlog (512 slots).
  6. At ~200 records/sec, ~48 appends queue during the 242 ms lock hold.
  7. If the backlog fills before the sweeper releases, send() connects time out (1 s timeout).
  8. send() returns False. The hook is fire-and-forget — the agent doesn't retry. The record is lost.

Over 100 seconds of soak, the sweeper runs 20 times (every 5 s). Each sweep blocks ~48 appends. 20 × 48 = 960 blocked appends. 9,036 of 10,000 delivered. 964 silently lost.

The agent doesn't know. send() returns False, but the hook is fire-and-forget — the agent ignores the return value. The daemon doesn't log the dropped sends. The store has 9,036 records instead of 10,000, and the only way to notice is to count.

The fix that wasn't a fix

The first diagnosis was wrong, and it cost two full test runs.

"The single-threaded accept path is the bottleneck." The listen backlog was 128, so it got raised:

# Before
server.listen(128)

# After
server.listen(512)

Result: 9,499/10,000 (95%). Better. Still dropping 500.

The first run before any backlog change was 9,016/10,000 (90%). Raising to 512 moved it to 9,499 (95%). The improvement was real but the problem was unchanged — more queue room just meant more sends waited longer before timing out. The drop rate went from 10% to 5%, but 500 records still vanished.

The diagnosis was "the accept path can't keep up." The actual problem was "the accept path is blocked." Those look the same from the outside — sends are being dropped — but the fix is completely different. The first says "make the accept path faster or give it more room." The second says "stop holding the lock it needs."

Because more backlog doesn't prevent drops — it delays them. The bottleneck was never queue capacity. It was the time append() spent blocked on the lock. More backlog means more sends queue before timing out, but they still time out if the sweeper holds the lock long enough.

tip: Raising a backlog, pool size, or buffer to "fix" a performance issue is usually a band-aid. If the bottleneck is lock-hold time, more queue room just delays the drops. Measure the lock-hold time before you touch the queue.

Two full suite runs went to a band-aid before the actual lock got measured.

The right fix: snapshot, then verify

Move the expensive work out of the critical section. Read and verify without the lock, then swap the in-memory reference under the lock — O(1):

def refresh(self):
    entries = self._load()                  # disk read — no lock
    status = self._verify_entries(entries)  # O(n) verify — no lock

    with self._lock:                        # O(1) reference swap
        if len(entries) >= len(self._entries):
            self._entries = entries
        self._recount()
    return status

The lock now covers a pointer assignment instead of 242 ms of work. The accept thread never blocks for more than microseconds.

tip: Never hold a lock the hot path needs while doing O(n) work. Snapshot under the lock, process outside it, swap the reference in O(1). The work doesn't get faster — the critical section gets 242 ms smaller.

Result: 10,000/10,000 delivered. p99 = 0.36 ms. verify-store green.

The second bug the fix introduced

The very next run after that change failed:

agentsec-agentwatch: chain broken at seq 815

Moving the read outside the lock introduced a race. The disk read (_load()) runs without the lock. While it's reading, append() may write new entries to the file. The disk read can complete before those writes land, producing a shorter entry list — 815 entries instead of 820.

If refresh() then replaces self._entries with this shorter list, the next append() computes seq = 815 + 1 = 816 and prev_hash = entries[815].hash. But entry 816 was already written to disk by the append() that happened during the disk read. Now there are two entries with seq 816 on disk. The chain is broken.

The fix is the length guard:

if len(entries) >= len(self._entries):   # never adopt a stale, shorter snapshot
    self._entries = entries

If the disk snapshot is shorter than what's in memory, keep memory. Verification still runs on the snapshot — and may detect tampering — but the in-memory state is not corrupted. The next sweep picks up whatever it missed.

This is the subtle cost of moving work outside a lock. When the lock protected both the read and the swap, the snapshot was always consistent with memory by construction. When the read happens unlocked, the snapshot can be stale — and "stale" means "shorter than reality" in an append-only store. The length guard turns a potential chain break into a benign missed sweep.

The scaling table

The total refresh() time is the same — the file read and verification still take O(n). What changed is what is locked:

Store entries refresh() total time Lock held for
1,000 11 ms ~0 ms (reference swap)
5,000 56 ms ~0 ms
10,000 116 ms ~0 ms
20,000 242 ms ~0 ms

The work didn't get faster. The critical section got 242 ms smaller.

What I keep repeating to myself

O(n) under a contended lock is a scaling cliff. It works at low n, fails at high n, and fails silently and load-dependently — invisible in unit tests, visible only under sustained load.

Silent data loss is worse than a crash. A crash is visible. A dropped record with a success response is a lie the operator can't see. At least a crash tells you something broke.

The symptom doesn't point at the cause. "Sends are being dropped" sends you to the network, the backlog, the accept loop. The real cause was lock contention in a background thread. Per-thread timing is what diagnoses it.

It's fixed in agentwatch v0.1.0, and the 10k soak is the regression test that keeps it fixed.

The question worth asking of your own system: what's the lock-hold time of your background work at 10× your current scale? If it hasn't been measured, it's probably the thing blocking the hot path.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.1.0 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • Suite: agentic-suite — the full set of agent-security tools
  • Field test report (defect D-1, FT-28)
  • Soak evidence: FT-28/
  • Store: store.py

articles.title: Sherlock Holmes: Why Prewarming a Voice Agent Didn't Make the First Reply Faster
articles.description: This is one case from the Sherlock Holmes series. Each write-up is a production problem me had to...
articles.body_html:
This is one case from the Sherlock Holmes series. Each write-up is a production problem me had to take apart. feel free to checkout other blogs.

This one did not start as a latency mystery. It started as a bill.

We prewarm a voice agent before the call connects. You send the model a request early, and you open the speech sockets early, so that if a person picks up, the first reply is already on its way. You pay a little up front, and the caller is not supposed to sit in silence while everything wakes up. That is the whole idea, and for a long time we treated it as obviously worth it.

Then we looked at where the LLM money was actually going. Almost 60% of the voice agent's model cost was the prewarm. Not the turns where someone was talking to the agent. The request we fired in case they might.

So the first question was not whether prewarm was fast. It was who we were warming up for.

The calls were not conversations

Once we split a day's calls open, they did not look like the conversations we thought we were paying to speed up. About 28% ended before the agent had played a single message. Another 63% got as far as the greeting and then nothing came back. The caller never spoke. Most of what was left was over inside one or two turns. Voicemail, no answer, or someone who picked up and cut the line straight away.

We had already paid the model to get ready for calls that never became a conversation.

Retries made that impossible to miss. Out of 48,103 calls that day, 32,244 were first attempts and 15,859 were retries, about a third. Of those retries, 15,143 failed, voicemail or no answer. About 95% of the time a retry was the same dead call again. If you warm every one of those, you are paying a model request on a pile of calls that are very unlikely to have a person waiting on the other end.

That was a small enough change to try. We left prewarm on for ordinary calls and turned it off for retries. After that we were simply not paying for the voicemail, the no-answer, and the calls that ended the moment they connected.

Once the change had been out for a bit, we went back and analysed the calls. Ordinary calls still had the prewarm. Retries did not. The cost side looked the way we hoped. Then one thing in the latency did not.

Both groups were almost the same.

That felt fishy. The prewarm was supposed to be why the first reply came out faster, so the retries, running without it, should have been the slow ones. They were not. I did not want to shrug at a chart, so I dug into the calls behind it.

What came out was a p50 of 1,235 ms with prewarm off and 1,163 ms with it on. About 72 ms. p95 was 2,118 ms against 2,149 ms. We watched the same split over the next days, prewarm completed on one side and prewarm skipped on the other, and the two lines still sat together.

Production traffic moves a lot of things at once, so I did not want to stop there. I took the production prewarm and the first-turn request, put them in a small script, and ran both ways on a VM. One run let the prime finish. The other skipped it. The speed came back about the same. Not much in it either way.

That is the part that took a while to sit right, because the cache was doing its job. On the GPT-5.1 prewarm replies, about 98% hit the cache, and around 70% of the prompt tokens were billed as cached. The prompt was warm. The caller still waited. We went looking for anyone else who had measured this, and Vlad Iliescu's notes on prompt caching with Azure OpenAI landed in the same place. He cached the prompt and still did not see a real jump in speed, because the reply is generated again every time. A cache hit only means the model did not have to read the prompt again. The reply is new on every call, so it still has to be generated, token by token, and that is the wait the caller feels. You can have a high cache rate, and you can spend real money keeping that prefix warm, and the first sentence still arrives when the generation finishes. The prewarm was not a head start they could hear. It was a bill for a prefix.

Once that stayed true past a single day, we stopped treating it as a retry tweak and turned the LLM prewarm off for every call.

The speech path was telling the same story

Taking the model prewarm off is what finally pushed us into the rest of the code. Speech to text and text to speech were being warmed too, and we had left them alone because a socket you open early sounds like a socket you will not have to open later. Worth reading the code before you believe that.

Speech to text went first, and it fell apart as soon as we followed the socket. While the phone is still ringing we open a second Deepgram connection, and when the person answers we close it. The call is not listening on that connection. LiveKit has already opened the socket the audio actually flows through, so the one we opened for prewarm never receives the caller's voice. We open it, the call connects, we close it, and nothing they said has passed through it. It might still warm a DNS lookup or a TLS handshake. On bulk calling, the call before this one has usually done that already. There is no audio path being reused. We had been warming a socket that could not hear.

Text to speech is the place the idea is actually real, which is why it is worth not throwing the whole thing out here. For some providers, the warmup opens a WebSocket and leaves that connection ready. When the agent speaks the first line, it uses the connection that is already open instead of dialing a new one. That is a real head start, and it is what these providers do: Cartesia, ElevenLabs, Deepgram TTS, Sarvam, Fish Audio, and Soniox.

Two of them do not do that. With Inworld, the warmup only sets aside an empty pool. The WebSocket is still opened when the first line is generated, which is the moment you were hoping to have already got past. With OpenAI, the warmup sends a light HTTP request and keeps no connection at all. By the time the agent has something to say, both of them are starting cold. We had been counting that warmup as done, and for those two nothing was being held open for the first line.

Where it landed

Follow it back and the three findings are one story. We were paying to get ready for calls nobody answered, the model warmup was not making the first reply faster, and two of the speech warmups were not holding anything the call could use.

So the LLM prewarm stays off. The speech-to-text prewarm comes out with it, because a second socket that never hears the caller is not a warmup. Text-to-speech prewarm stays, but only where the provider really does keep a connection waiting. Where the warmup only sets aside an empty pool, or pings and hangs up, we stop doing it.

That is the part I would want you to take from this. The bill was mostly for calls that had already ended.

Have you hit the same thing? A warmup, or a cached prompt, that looked fine on your side while the person on the call still waited. If you have, I would like to hear how it showed up for you.

articles.title: Zeen: A New Systems Programming Language with a Comptime Engine
articles.description: Website: zeen-lang.tech Github: mealet/zeen  (Would appreciate if you'd leave a star on Github)      ...
articles.body_html:
Website: zeen-lang.tech
Github: mealet/zeen

(Would appreciate if you'd leave a star on Github)

What is Zeen

Zeen - a modern systems programming language designed for simplicity, safety, and predictable control over memory. It provides toolchains and compiler rules to operate data easily and drop it automatically after usage with move semantics to avoid any runtime overhead. The main idea is to create a tool to develop efficient software where most errors are caught at compile time.

Zeen took many design choices from Rust and Zig programming languages, which makes it more familiar for most developers. Besides that it introduces its own approach to ownership, memory management, and compile-time execution.

Development Tools

Besides compiler and set of libraries (core, std), Zeen has:

  • Editors plugins for VS Code and Neovim
  • Package manager Zora

Small Example 

fn print_this[T: Display](value: T) {
  @println("Yeah, I've printed this: {}", value);
}

fn main() {
  print_this(123);
  print_this("hello!");
}

Quick Start

  1. Install latest release following official guide from documentation.
  2. Create new project with Zora: 
zora new my_project
cd my_project
  1. Write code and run your binary package: 
zora run

New Comptime Engine

Last update v0.4.0 brought a lot of enhancements: frontend performance, new warnings system, new macros, fixed C ABI and Comptime Engine.

Zeen's comptime engine allows you to move some evaluations or constructions away from runtime to the compiler.

You can define and eval constants, create Comptime functions which can construct new types, export expressions and declarations, emit declarations into current scope, format print at the compile time and more. Here's some examples of it.

Simple constants and splicing:

comptime N = 16;
comptime SquaredN = N * N;

fn main() {
  @println("{} -> {}", N, SquaredN);
  @println("$(N) -> $(SquaredN)");
}

Advanced usage (declarations, type values and etc):

comptime fn pair_of(struct_name: comptime_str, a: zeen_type, b: zeen_type) zeen_decl {
  @zeen_decl(
    struct $(struct_name) {
      pub a: $(a),
      pub b: $(b),
    }
  )
}

comptime {
  @emit(pair_of("NumsPair", i32, f32));
}

fn main() {
  let pair = NumsPair { .a = 1, .b = 1.0 };
  @println("{} {}", pair.a, pair.b);
}

See more info and examples on changelog and comptime docs pages.

articles.title: Deno 2.9's task cache turns a 4-second build into a 10-millisecond skip
articles.description: I measured Deno's new deno task caching: 3.9s cold against 9ms warm on a real build step, but a 3000-file input tree made the cache check itself about 4x slower than running an untracked task.
articles.body_html:
A deno.json task with a files list now remembers whether it needs to run at all. I hadn't seen this mentioned anywhere, so I built a small, deliberately expensive build step, ran it with and without the new caching fields, and tried to break it.

The short version: a task that took 3.9 to 4.3 seconds dropped to under 10 milliseconds once nothing in its declared inputs had changed. That part works as advertised. What doesn't work the way I expected is the cost of checking in the first place, and what happens when a task writes to a file it also lists as an input.

What the feature actually is

Deno's task runner (deno task, driven by the tasks block in deno.json) now accepts three extra fields on a task definition:

{
  "tasks": {
    "build": {
      "command": "deno run --allow-read --allow-write build.ts",
      "files": ["src/**/*.txt", "build.ts"],
      "output": ["dist/**"]
    }
  }
}
  • files is the input glob. Declaring it is what turns caching on at all; a task with no files field always runs.
  • output is the glob of files the task produces. On a cache hit, these get restored from the cache store rather than regenerated.
  • env (not shown above) lists environment variable names whose values also feed the fingerprint.

I ran this against Deno 2.9.8, installed from the official Linux x86_64 build, with no --unstable flag anywhere. This is shipped, stable behaviour, not a preview.

The headline number

My build.ts reads every file under src/, hashes each one 2000 times with SHA-256 to simulate real CPU-bound work, and writes a combined manifest to dist/. Forty source files, about 1.1MB total.

Run Cold (cache cleared first) Warm (cache hit)
1 4.289s 0.0100s
2 4.025s 0.0093s
3 3.939s 0.0100s

Fastest cold run against fastest warm run: 3.939s versus 0.0093s, a 423x difference. All three warm runs printed the same line:

Task build deno run --allow-read --allow-write build.ts (cached, inputs unchanged)

No process spawn for deno run, no re-read of the source files, no re-hashing. The task is simply not executed.

It really is content, not timestamps

The cache manifest, which lives under ~/.cache/deno/task_cache_v1/<hash>/manifest.json, records a size and an mtime for every tracked file alongside a content_hash and a static_hash. Seeing mtime sitting right there in the JSON, I assumed it was part of what decided a cache hit, the way plenty of build tools work.

I ran touch src/file_5.txt with no edit to the file's contents, then ran the task again:

Task build deno run --allow-read --allow-write build.ts (cached, inputs unchanged)

Still cached. Then I actually appended a line to the same file and ran it again:

Task build deno run --allow-read --allow-write build.ts
build.ts actually ran

That re-ran, and the following run went back to cached. So the documentation's claim ("the contents of the matching files") holds up under a direct test: mtime and size are a cheap pre-check to decide whether a file is worth reading, not the thing that decides the final verdict. A bare timestamp bump doesn't invalidate anything.

Output really does get restored, not just skipped

The other claim worth checking: that deleting your output directory and re-running a cached task regenerates it. I deleted dist/ entirely, ran the cached task again, and dist/main.txt came back with the exact content the last real build produced, while build.log (a side effect outside the declared output glob, used only to prove whether the command itself re-ran) stayed untouched. The command did not execute. The files were pulled back from the cache store. Both halves of the claim check out.

Where it quietly never helps you

I wrote a task whose files glob included a file that the command itself appends to:

{
  "tasks": {
    "selfmutate": {
      "command": "echo appended >> src/input.txt && echo ran",
      "files": ["src/*.txt"]
    }
  }
}

Run it three times and src/input.txt ends with three "appended" lines. Every run changes the very input it's fingerprinted against, so every run invalidates its own next run. Nothing in the tool warns you about this. If your build step writes a log, a timestamp, or a generated file into the same directory it reads from, caching silently does nothing for you, and you'd have no way to tell short of watching the task actually execute every time.

Two things that used to be bugs and aren't anymore

Deno's own commit history shows a real defect here: for a while, deno task build foo and deno task build bar produced the same fingerprint, because the hash only covered the command string, not the arguments appended after it. I tested this directly on 2.9.8 with a task that just echoes its arguments:

$ deno task argtask -- foo    # first run: executes
$ deno task argtask -- foo    # second run: cached
$ deno task argtask -- bar    # different arg: executes again, correctly

Different arguments get different fingerprints now. Same story for env: a task with "env": ["MODE"] ran fresh under MODE=dev, cached on the repeat, then ran fresh again the moment I switched to MODE=prod, then cached again on the repeat of that. Both the documented behaviour and a previously real bug check out against the current release.

What it costs when the task itself is cheap

This is the finding that argues against the headline number. I built a 3000-file, 12MB input tree and attached it to a task that does nothing but echo noop:

with files tracking (cache hit) no files field at all
Run 1 0.0320s 0.0101s
Run 2 0.0314s 0.0080s
Run 3 0.0346s 0.0106s

Checking whether 3000 files changed cost roughly 3 to 4 times longer than just running the command with no tracking at all, even on a hit. For my 4-second hashing job this overhead is noise. For a task that's already fast, say a lint pass over a small package that finishes in 20ms, attaching files over a large tree could plausibly cost more than it saves. Deno checks file size and modification time before reading contents, which keeps the common case cheap, but on a big enough tree that pre-check alone adds up.

No concurrency protection, and no partial reset

I started the same cold build task from two processes at once, with the cache cleared beforehand:

A: ELAPSED 3.9316s  (actually ran)
B: ELAPSED 4.0020s  (actually ran)

Both ran the full 4-second task in parallel. Nothing serialised them, and nothing let the second one wait for the first and reuse its result. If two CI steps or two editor saves trigger the same expensive task at once, you pay for it twice, not once.

There's also no way to invalidate a single task's cache entry. deno task has no --no-cache flag. The only lever is deno clean, which removes the entire DENO_DIR, not just task_cache_v1:

$ deno clean
Removed /root/.cache/deno (24 files, 607.61KB)

That also wipes the module cache, the npm cache, and everything else Deno stores, which on a real project is a much bigger rebuild than just re-running one build step.

What I got wrong on the way

My first assumption, reading the cache manifest before running a single test, was that the stored mtime field was load-bearing: that touching a file would be enough to force a rebuild, because that's how make and a lot of task runners behave. It isn't. The manifest stores mtime as a cheap filter to decide whether to bother reading a file at all; the actual cache decision rests on the content hash underneath it. I only caught this because I tested the boring case (touch, no edit) before the interesting one (real edit), rather than assuming they'd behave the same.

Run it yourself

This needs only the Deno binary, no Docker and no account:

curl -fsSL https://deno.land/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.deno/bin:$PATH"
deno --version   # I used 2.9.8

mkdir deno-cache-test && cd deno-cache-test
mkdir src
for i in $(seq 1 40); do head -c 20000 </dev/urandom | base64 > "src/file_$i.txt"; done

cat > build.ts <<'EOF'
const files = [];
for (const entry of Deno.readDirSync("src")) if (entry.isFile) files.push(`src/${entry.name}`);
files.sort();
let combined = "";
for (const f of files) {
  let digest = await Deno.readFile(f);
  for (let i = 0; i < 2000; i++) {
    digest = new Uint8Array(await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", digest));
  }
  combined += `${f} ${Array.from(digest).map(b => b.toString(16).padStart(2,"0")).join("")}\n`;
}
await Deno.mkdir("dist", { recursive: true });
await Deno.writeTextFile("dist/manifest.txt", combined);
console.error("build.ts actually ran");
EOF

cat > deno.json <<'EOF'
{
  "tasks": {
    "build": {
      "command": "deno run --allow-read --allow-write build.ts",
      "files": ["src/**/*.txt", "build.ts"],
      "output": ["dist/**"]
    }
  }
}
EOF

time deno task build   # cold: several seconds
time deno task build   # warm: single-digit milliseconds

If you want to see the self-mutation pitfall, add a task whose command appends to a file matched by its own files glob, and watch it execute on every run regardless.

What to do with this

Point files only at what the specific task actually reads, never at src/** for a whole repo when the task touches one package, and check first that the command doesn't also write into that same glob, or caching will quietly do nothing for it. And before adding this to something that already runs in under 50ms, time it cold and warm the way I did above. On my 3000-file tree, the fingerprint check alone cost more than that.

articles.title: I built a motion graphics editor that runs in a browser tab (and let an AI animate in it)
articles.description: Keyframes, easing, multi-track audio, 4K export, and a live link that lets an AI agent edit the project while you watch. Here's how Riptide works, and the one-word CSS bug that broke the whole window.
articles.body_html:
Every time I needed a 15-second animated clip, I had two options: pay for a motion graphics suite I would open twice a month, or fight a template site that exports a watermark.

So I built my own. It's called Riptide, and it runs in a browser tab.

It's not a toy. The promo Short for it was made in it. Here is what it does, how it is built, and the bug that taught me the most.

What it does

Layers and keyframes. Rectangles, ellipses, polygons, stars, arcs, waves, text, images and video. Any property can be keyframed: position, size, rotation, scale, opacity, colour, blur, stroke. There are 23 easing curves, plus ready-made presets like Pop in, Rise, Typewriter and Draw on that you drag onto a layer.

A real timeline. Zoom, per-property keyframe rows, trim bars, split at the playhead, markers, and snapping to the playhead, markers, keyframes and clip edges.

Audio that behaves. Multiple tracks that play together. Drag clips, trim them, split them, and drag the little dots on a clip's corners to fade in and out. Every track gets mixed into the export, fades and volumes included.

Design tools you expect. Multi-select with Shift-click or a selection box, align and distribute, centre on canvas, and an aspect-ratio lock that images get by default so you never squash a photo by accident.

Export. MP4, WebM, GIF, a PNG sequence or a still, up to 4K.

How it's built

The whole editor is plain JavaScript drawing to a single <canvas> with the 2D context. No framework, no WebGL.

Every frame is rendered from scratch by one function:

function renderScene(c, t, scale = 1) {
  c.setTransform(scale, 0, 0, scale, 0, 0);
  c.fillStyle = S.bg; c.fillRect(0, 0, S.w, S.h);
  for (const L of S.layers) if (visibleAt(L, t)) {
    c.save(); c.globalCompositeOperation = L.blend || 'source-over';
    drawLayer(c, L, t); c.restore();
  }
}

That one decision paid off over and over. The editor preview, the fullscreen viewer, the exporter and the frames an AI agent looks at all call the same function with a different context and scale. If it looks right in the editor, it exports right.

The backend is a small Flask server whose main job is handing frames to ffmpeg. The browser renders each frame and uploads it, then the server hands the frames to ffmpeg with the audio tracks mixed in, fades included. A PNG sequence export does not even need ffmpeg.

Keyboard shortcuts live in one table:

['Align', 'Centre on canvas', 'alt+c', () => centerOnCanvas('xy')],
['Edit',  'Select all layers', 'mod+a', () => selectAll()],

That table drives the shortcuts, the cheat sheet and the command palette, so the three can never disagree.

The part people ask about: an AI that animates live

Riptide has a built-in MCP server. Any agent that speaks MCP can connect to the open project and work in it: add layers, set keyframes, apply presets, align things, add audio, and render a frame to look at its own work.

The important design choice: agent edits go through the exact same path as yours. They show up on the canvas instantly, they can be undone with Cmd+Z, and the file is marked as edited. The agent isn't generating a file you import later. It is a second pair of hands in the same document.

Asking an agent to "make the title pop in on the beat and centre everything" and watching it happen on screen is the closest thing to magic I've built.

The bug that broke the whole window

My favorite bug from this project was one word long.

Dragging the divider between the Layers and Media panels made the entire window flicker between the normal layout and a scrambled one. I fixed the obvious suspect first: a feedback loop where the panel scrolled, the measurement shifted, and the next size came out wrong. Still broken.

The real cause: while you dragged, the code added a class to <body> to show the resize cursor. The class for vertical resizing was row.

The app already had a .row class. It styles the little input fields in the side panel:

.row { display: flex; height: 26px; }

So for the length of every drag, the whole page became a 26-pixel-tall flex row.

The fix was to stop putting generic class names on <body> and use a namespaced attribute instead:

document.documentElement.dataset.resizing = axis;   // 'x' or 'y'

html[data-resizing] { user-select: none; }
html[data-resizing=y] body::after { cursor: row-resize; }

The lesson I took away: state on <html> or <body> is global, so name it like a global. And when a test measures sizes but never looks at the screen mid-drag, it can pass while the user watches the page collapse.

What I would tell you if you're building something similar

  1. Render everything from one function. Preview, export and thumbnails should never have their own drawing code.
  2. Make the agent use the user's edit path. Undo, dirty state and live updates come for free, and you never have two sources of truth.
  3. Measure from the start of a drag, not the live layout. Anything that re-reads the layout mid-drag can feed back into itself.
  4. Look at the screen. Numbers in a test log are not the same as what a person sees.

What would you want to see in a browser-based motion editor? And if you've hit a one-word CSS bug that took down a whole page, I want to hear it in the comments.

The repo is Natuworkguy/Riptide on GitHub.

articles.title: Cookie-Dependent Content and SEO: Test the Page Without Yesterday's State
articles.description: To diagnose cookie-dependent content for SEO, inspect a public page as a fresh visitor and compare it...
articles.body_html:
To diagnose cookie-dependent content for SEO, inspect a public page as a fresh visitor and compare it with the returning visit your team normally sees. Check the initial response and rendered content separately. If the important answer appears only after remembered state is restored, the familiar browser view may be hiding a discovery problem.

Google documents a specific reason to make this check: its Web Rendering Service does not retain state across page loads, and storage and cookies are cleared across loads. That is documented Google behavior, not a claim about every AI engine. The workflow below investigates the page without bypassing consent, authentication or access controls.

Choose one public answer to trace

Use a concrete content target. Imagine a fictional scheduling product whose public integrations page should explain whether its calendar connection supports two-way updates. Returning visitors see the explanation. A fresh browser shows a short introduction and an empty space where the integration details should be.

The target is that public explanation, not every visual element on the page. Record its expected wording, the URL, the relevant preference state and how a person reaches it. This makes it possible to distinguish a missing buyer answer from a decorative component that merely loads later.

Keep the scope public. A customer's private calendar, account settings and paid application workspace are not material you should expose for SEO. If the answer belongs behind authentication, investigate the public documentation that describes the capability rather than trying to make the private workspace crawlable.

Separate the response from the rendered page

The initial HTML response and the browser's rendered document answer different questions. The response shows what the server sent for the request. The rendered document shows what exists after the browser has executed the page's permitted scripts and processed the resulting changes.

In the fictional example, the response might contain the integration heading but no capability explanation. The returning browser might later populate that explanation from an application component. That observation narrows the investigation; it does not prove a search engine failed to render it.

Use the browser's normal developer inspection tools to examine both views. Note whether the text is absent, present but hidden, or replaced after a preference is loaded. Avoid diagnosing the whole site from a screenshot. A screenshot establishes what was visible in that state, while the response and document help explain how the page reached it.

Compare fresh and returning visits deliberately

Open the public page in a clean browsing session using the site's normal access flow. Record what happens before any optional preference is chosen, then record the result of an appropriate normal choice. Separately inspect the returning session that originally looked correct.

Do not silently change the experiment halfway through. If language, region, consent or sign-in state differs, write that down. A fresh visitor in one locale and a returning visitor in another are not a controlled comparison of cookies alone.

The useful question is whether a prior visit is required for the public answer to exist. If the answer appears after an ordinary action, document that action. If it needs a preference stored during an earlier page load, identify that dependency. At this stage, describe the behavior you can reproduce rather than naming a cause you have not established.

Use Google's rendering evidence for the Google question

Google's JavaScript troubleshooting documentation describes its stateless rendering behavior. It also points to URL Inspection and the Rich Results Test for examining rendered output and related rendering problems. Use the available owner tools and permissions for the site you are auditing.

Compare the relevant text in that rendered evidence with the fresh and returning browser observations. Save the test date and tested URL. A difference deserves investigation; it does not by itself tell you whether cookies, blocked resources, timing or another condition caused it.

Keep this evidence tied to Google Search. A Google rendering test is not a measurement of what ChatGPT, Claude or another answer surface retrieved. It can reveal a public-page problem worth fixing, but engine-specific claims need engine-specific evidence. This boundary prevents a useful technical diagnosis from turning into an unsupported universal AI crawler rule.

Trace the dependency before choosing the repair

Ask the responsible developer where the public text comes from and what conditions allow it to render. In the fictional integration page, perhaps the application waits for a remembered display preference before mounting a component that contains both optional features and essential documentation.

If that dependency is confirmed, the design question becomes smaller: can the public explanation be delivered through the normal public page without requiring yesterday's state? The solution might involve separating essential documentation from an optional interactive component. The appropriate implementation depends on the actual system; this article does not prescribe a framework-specific patch.

Do not solve the problem by serving secret extra claims only to bots. Do not remove required consent protections, expose private data or make a paid feature public to create a successful test. The goal is consistent access to information the business already intends to publish.

Repair the user journey as well as the content dependency

A page can contain the right text and still leave a first-time visitor unable to use it. Check the visible route to the explanation. Does the heading describe the integration question? Does the page state the current support conditions? Can a person reach the relevant documentation without remembering a previous selection?

For the fictional calendar connection, a useful public answer might identify which direction of updates is supported and link to current setup limitations. Those product facts must be verified before publication. Adding a generic paragraph about integration benefits would not repair the missing capability answer.

Keep preference-specific variations understandable. If the site offers localized instructions, explain how a fresh visitor selects the applicable version. Avoid treating every variation as a bug. The issue is an unintended dependency that makes a public answer unavailable or misleading, not the mere existence of a preference.

Retest the same states after the change

Repeat the initial response check, the clean visit and the returning visit against the same content target. Also repeat the relevant Google inspection when available. Capture the text that matters, the URL, date, browser conditions and any actions required to reveal it.

A useful acceptance statement is specific: the public integration explanation is present for a fresh visitor under the intended conditions, and the returning experience still works. This is stronger than saying “SEO fixed,” because it names the behavior actually verified.

Google's technical requirements also make clear that meeting requirements does not guarantee indexing. A successful rendering repair is therefore not proof of an indexing gain, a ranking gain or an AI citation. Track those outcomes separately if they matter to the project.

Leave a diagnosis the next person can repeat

Write a short investigation note with the public question, expected text, tested states, observed differences, confirmed dependency and completed repair. Include what remains unknown. A small record with evidence is more useful than a ticket that says the page looked different in incognito mode.

If the problem cannot be reproduced, retain the original conditions rather than forcing a conclusion. A browser extension, an old session or another environmental difference may need further checking. Report an unresolved discrepancy as unresolved.

For search and AI visibility work, the practical payoff is a more dependable public source. Buyers and search systems still have to discover, interpret and choose that source. Testing without remembered state addresses one concrete failure mode: a team mistaking its familiar returning-user view for the page that a first-time visitor can actually read.
