articles.title: Java Erases Your Generics. TypeScript Erases Every Type. What Survives to Runtime
articles.description: Java keeps classes and generic signatures in bytecode. TypeScript keeps almost nothing. Which JVM habits break, and what replaces them.
articles.body_html:
• Book: Kotlin and Java to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

If you have written Java for a while, you have hit this wall at least once. You type list instanceof ArrayList<Integer> and the compiler refuses. The Oracle generics tutorial gives the reason in one line: "The runtime does not keep track of type parameters, so it cannot tell the difference between an ArrayList and an ArrayList."

You learned to live with it. You use ArrayList<?>, you pass a Class<T> around, you reach for Jackson's TypeReference when a List<User> has to come out of JSON.

Then you move to TypeScript, write if (value instanceof User) against an interface, and get 'User' only refers to a type, but is being used as a value here (a walkthrough of that error). Same family of problem, much bigger blast radius. Java erases your generics. TypeScript erases every type you write. The useful question is what is still there when the program runs, in each language, and what you do about the gap.

What javac erases, and what it quietly keeps

The Java tutorial on type erasure lists three things the compiler does: it replaces every type parameter with its bound, or Object if it has none; it inserts casts where they are needed for type safety; and it generates bridge methods so polymorphism still works in generic subclasses. The result, in the tutorial's words, is bytecode that "contains only ordinary classes, interfaces, and methods."

Take three lines:

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("ada");
String first = names.get(0);

Run javap -c on the compiled class and the call to get goes to the erased List, whose get returns Object. The String you see in your source survives only as the cast the compiler inserted after the call. List<String> and List<Integer> run as the same class.

That is the part every JVM developer knows. The part people forget is how much Java keeps.

First, every object knows its own class. The TypeScript team's own guide for Java and C# programmers puts it plainly: in Java "any given value or object has one exact type", and you can call value.getClass() to ask for it.

Second, declarations keep their generics. The class file format has a Signature attribute that "stores a signature for a class, interface, constructor, method, field, or record component whose declaration in the Java programming language uses type variables or parameterized types." javap -v prints the Signature attribute, and reflection reads them: Field.getGenericType() must return a Type that "accurately reflect[s] the actual type arguments used in the source code."

Neal Gafter, who introduced super type tokens in a 2006 post, summed it up in a reply in that post's comments: "The STATIC types are recorded in the bytecodes, but not the dynamic types." A List<String> object has forgotten its String. A field declared as List<String> has not.


Java forgets the type arguments on values but keeps classes and declared signatures. TypeScript keeps neither.

What tsc erases: everything that is only a type

TypeScript's handbook has a section literally named Erased Types, and it ends on a note: "Type annotations never change the runtime behavior of your program."

Here is a small file with the usual suspects:

interface User { id: string; email: string }
type Users = User[];

function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined {
  return xs[0];
}

class Mailer {
  send(to: User): string {
    return `mail to ${to.email}`;
  }
}

Strip what is TypeScript-only and this is the JavaScript that remains (with a modern target, so the template literal stays as is):

function first(xs) {
  return xs[0];
}

class Mailer {
  send(to) {
    return `mail to ${to.email}`;
  }
}

User is gone. Users is gone. T is gone, with no Object stand-in and no inserted cast. The parameter annotation on send is gone. What survives is what was already JavaScript: the function and the class. The guide for OOP programmers says of an interface that it "is not present in any form at runtime", and that "information about e.g. the instantiation of a generic type parameter is not available at runtime." There is no Signature attribute equivalent. Nothing is recorded on the declaration either.

There is one opt-in way to record something: with emitDecoratorMetadata, tsc records a decorated member's type as a runtime reference, and NestJS dependency injection reads it. It records Array for a User[] and Object for an interface, so the generic and the interface are still gone.

Two TypeScript features do leave runtime code. Enums "are real objects that exist at runtime". The handbook shows enum Enum { A } compiling to an object with both directions mapped:

"use strict";
var Enum;
(function (Enum) {
    Enum[Enum["A"] = 0] = "A";
})(Enum || (Enum = {}));

const enum goes the other way: members are inlined at the use site and the declaration is "completely removed during compilation." Namespaces with values and constructor parameter properties also emit code.

That short list is shrinking in practice. Node.js now runs .ts files by stripping types by default since v22.18.0 and v23.6.0. It "will replace TypeScript syntax with whitespace, and no type checking is performed," and it rejects enums, namespaces with runtime code and parameter properties because those need a transform. TypeScript 5.8 added --erasableSyntaxOnly so the compiler flags the same constructs. TypeScript is drifting toward JavaScript plus annotations a runtime can delete.

Side by side:

At runtime Java TypeScript
Class of an object yes, getClass() only if built with new from a class
Generic args on a declaration yes, Signature attribute no
Generic args on a value no no
Interfaces yes, as class files no
Type aliases n/a no
Enums yes yes, unless const enum

Four Java habits that stop working

Overloading by type. Java lets you write describe(Card c) and describe(Iban i) as two methods and let the compiler pick. The TypeScript handbook on overloads describes something else: several overload signatures followed by a single implementation, whose signature "is not visible from the outside." There is one function body at runtime. If the two cases need different logic, that body has to look at the value and branch. (Java has its own edge here, by the way: you cannot overload print(Set<String>) and print(Set<Integer>), because the tutorial notes they "would all share the same classfile representation.")

instanceof on an interface. In Java, interfaces compile to class files and obj instanceof Payable works. In TypeScript the interface has no runtime value, so the check does not compile. And instanceof on a class only walks the prototype chain. The guide is blunt that typeof and instanceof "are still working on the values as they exist in the type-erased output code." An object from JSON.parse that has every field of Account is still not an instanceof Account.

Reflection on generic parameters. There is no getGenericType() to call. A function like load<T>(key: string): T cannot look at T, so whatever it returns, the T is only the caller's promise; nothing checks it. A super type token has nothing to capture, because the declaration carries no signature.

Deserialization by class. Jackson's model is mapper.readValue(json, User.class), plus new TypeReference<List<Integer>>() { } for the generic cases, which works because of that Signature attribute. In TypeScript, User is usually an interface, so there is no User.class to hand to anything. Even if you make it a class, a nested User[] field has no element type recorded anywhere for a library to read.


Classes and enums make it through compilation. Interfaces, type aliases and generics do not.

What replaces them: put the type information in a value

Every replacement follows one rule. If you need to know something at runtime, it has to exist at runtime as a value. TypeScript then checks that value statically.

Discriminated unions replace overloads and class hierarchies. Give each case a literal field and switch on it. The narrowing chapter defines it: "When every type in a union contains a common property with literal types, TypeScript considers that to be a discriminated union."

type Payment =
  | { kind: "card"; last4: string }
  | { kind: "iban"; iban: string };

function describe(p: Payment): string {
  switch (p.kind) {
    case "card":
      return `card ending ${p.last4}`;
    case "iban":
      return `transfer from ${p.iban}`;
  }
}

The kind string is the runtime tag Java gave you for free with getClass(). You write it yourself, and the compiler narrows p in each branch.

User-defined type guards replace instanceof on interfaces. A function whose return type is a type predicate, parameterName is Type, tells the compiler what a true result proves:

function isUser(v: unknown): v is User {
  if (typeof v !== "object" || v === null) {
    return false;
  }
  const u = v as Record<string, unknown>;
  return typeof u.id === "string"
    && typeof u.email === "string";
}

The catch: the compiler trusts the predicate. If the body checks the wrong fields, nothing warns you. Keep guards short and next to the type they guard.

Runtime schemas replace readValue(json, User.class). This flips the direction. In Java you declare the class and the deserializer reads it. In TypeScript you declare a schema, which is a real runtime value, and derive the static type from it. With Zod, now on major version 4, that looks like this:

import { z } from "zod";

const User = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  email: z.string(),
});
type User = z.infer<typeof User>;

const result = User.safeParse(JSON.parse(body));
if (result.success) {
  console.log(result.data.email);
}

safeParse returns either the data or an error instead of throwing, and z.infer gives you the User type for the rest of the code. You write the declaration once and get both a runtime validator and a compile-time type. That is the closest thing TypeScript has to a reified class, and it works for nested arrays and unions, which is where User.class ran out on the JVM too.

A habit to keep instead

The JVM taught you to trust declared types at the boundary because the runtime would back them up with a ClassCastException. TypeScript will not. At every boundary where data enters (HTTP bodies, queue messages, localStorage, environment variables) the static type is only as true as the check you ran. Inside the boundary, after a schema or a guard has passed, the types are as reliable as Java's.

Inside your code, write types and let them vanish. At the edges, write values that check.

If this was useful

Erasure is one of those differences that looks like trivia until it breaks a habit you have had for ten years. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript is the book I wrote for that move. It walks a JVM developer through what changes on the way over: variance, null safety, sealed classes into unions, coroutines into async/await. It is part of The TypeScript Library:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

If you come from Java or Kotlin, start with book 3 in place of book 1, then go to The TypeScript Type System when the generics get deep. If you ship TypeScript at work, add TypeScript in Production.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: I Built Rillio: A JSX UI Runtime Using Addressable DOM Instead of Virtual DOM
articles.description: Exploring a different approach to DOM rendering with stable node identities, Flat Index, transactional patches, and JSX.
articles.body_html:
I've been working on a side project called Rillio, a small TypeScript/JSX UI runtime.

GitHub: https://github.com/vyquocvu/rillio

It started as an experiment. I was curious about one question:

What if DOM nodes had stable identities, and we could update them directly without relying on a Virtual DOM tree as the main source of truth?

React and Preact already solve UI rendering really well. SolidJS also showed that fine-grained reactivity can work without a traditional Virtual DOM.

So I'm not trying to reinvent React or claim I've built something faster than everything else.

I just wanted to explore a different architecture.

The idea: Addressable DOM / Flat Index

In Rillio, every managed DOM node gets a stable NodeId.

Instead of maintaining another authoritative component/VDOM tree describing the DOM structure, Rillio keeps a flat registry of nodes and their relationships.

A simplified version looks like this:

interface FlatNode {
  id: number;
  parentId: number | null;
  prevSibling: number | null;
  nextSibling: number | null;
  firstChild: number | null;
  lastChild: number | null;
  version: number;
  node: Node;
}

The actual implementation has more fields for ownership, lifecycle, boundaries and other things.

The important part is that a node can be accessed directly by ID.

const record = registry.getNode(nodeId);

No need to walk through a component tree just to locate the record.

Of course, looking up a node is only one small part of rendering. Structural changes, lifecycle management and keeping the registry in sync with the browser DOM are much harder problems.

One Patch Engine for DOM updates

Another design decision was to keep DOM mutations behind a single Patch Engine.

Something like:

tx.setText(nodeId, "Hello");
tx.move(nodeId, parentId, beforeId);
tx.remove(nodeId);

The runtime validates operations and applies them through a shared mutation path.

This gives Rillio a place to manage node ownership, ordering, versioning and cleanup.

It also makes debugging more interesting, since DOM changes can be described as operations rather than just arbitrary mutations scattered across the runtime.

But there is a tradeoff: transactions introduce their own complexity, especially around rollback, nested updates and callbacks.

I'm still working on those edge cases.

JSX stays familiar

I didn't want developers to learn a completely new syntax.

You can write components like this:

import { createRoot, useState } from "rillio";

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount(n => n + 1)}>
      Count: {count}
    </button>
  );
}

createRoot(document.getElementById("app")!)
  .render(<Counter />);

Looks pretty familiar, right?

But under the hood, Rillio uses its Flat Index and Patch Engine to manage DOM identity and updates.

It also has an explicit reactive DOM API for cases where I want more direct control over updates.

One thing worth mentioning: React-like syntax doesn't mean full React compatibility. That's not the goal right now.

Some interesting algorithm problems

This project turned out to involve more algorithms than I expected.

A few examples:

1. Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)

When reordering keyed lists, we want to preserve existing DOM nodes and avoid unnecessary moves.

LIS helps determine which nodes can stay in place.

For example:

Old: A B C D E
New: B D A C E

Instead of recreating the entire list, we can preserve the DOM nodes and move only the ones that need to change position.

2. Doubly linked siblings

Instead of storing child relationships only in arrays, the Flat Index tracks previous and next siblings.

This allows efficient linking and unlinking when the relevant nodes are already known.

3. Transaction validation

Before changing DOM structure, the runtime needs to check whether operations are valid.

For example, moving a parent into its own descendant should never be allowed.

4. Reactive dependency graphs

When state changes, ideally only the affected computations should run.

Things get tricky when dependencies change dynamically or multiple computations share the same dependencies.

5. Randomized consistency testing

This is probably one of my favorite parts.

I generate sequences of DOM updates and check whether the Flat Index still agrees with the actual DOM.

It's basically algorithm practice, except a bug might make half the UI disappear :)

What about performance?

I've been benchmarking Rillio against other UI runtimes, especially for keyed lists, text updates and DOM reordering.

Some scenarios look promising, particularly updates that benefit from stable node identity and minimal moves.

But there are also costs.

Maintaining a Flat Index requires additional metadata, and initial mounting has its own overhead.

So I don't think a single benchmark is enough to say one architecture is better.

I'm more interested in understanding which workloads benefit from this design, and which don't.

What's next?

Right now I'm focusing on correctness before adding more features.

A few things I want to improve:

  • Stronger transaction validation and rollback behavior
  • More randomized and model-based testing
  • Better handling of deeply nested DOM structures
  • Exploring cost-aware DOM patch planning
  • Investigating whether a compiler could optimize JSX into more direct DOM bindings

The long-term idea is to keep Addressable DOM as the foundation, while everything else — JSX, components, state and reactivity — works around it.

Final thoughts

Building a UI runtime from scratch has made me appreciate how many difficult problems existing frameworks already solve.

A simple counter is easy.

Keyed lists, lifecycle cleanup, focus preservation, nested updates, error recovery and keeping everything consistent? Not so easy.

I'm still not sure whether Addressable DOM will turn out to be a better architecture for real-world applications.

But thats exactly why I'm building it.

If you've worked on rendering engines, reactive systems or frontend frameworks, I'd really appreciate your thoughts.

Is a Flat Index actually a useful abstraction for UI rendering, or am I just moving complexity from one place to another?

Source code: https://github.com/vyquocvu/rillio

vyquocvu / rillio

Rillio is an experimental addressable-DOM runtime. It preserves familiar JSX authoring, while DOM identity, structure, ownership, and lifecycle are owned by a Flat Index rather than by a Virtual DOM tree.

Rillio is an experimental addressable-DOM runtime for client-side apps. JSX and explicit reactive views share one Flat Index and one transactional PatchEngine.

Install the published package in an existing app:

npm install @vyquocvu/rillio

See the package on npm for published versions and package details, or check out the standalone quickstart project.

Or clone the repository to run the examples locally:

cd rillio
npm install
npm run dev

articles.title: Your Next.js redirect() Silently Does Nothing Because It's Inside a try/catch
articles.description: A user fills in your form and clicks "Create post". The post is saved in the database. And the page...
articles.body_html:
A user fills in your form and clicks "Create post". The post is saved in the database. And the page shows "Could not create post".

They try again. Now there are two posts.

Nothing is wrong with your database. Your error handling caught something it was never supposed to catch.

The Code That Causes It 

// app/actions.ts
'use server';

import { redirect } from 'next/navigation';

export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
  try {
    const post = await db.post.create({
      data: { title: String(formData.get('title')) },
    });

    redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`);
  } catch (err) {
    return { error: 'Could not create post' };
  }
}

It reads perfectly. Save the post, go to its page, and if anything fails, return an error. A tidy, defensive pattern that you have probably written a hundred times in other frameworks.

Why It Breaks

In Next.js, redirect() does not return. It throws a special error, and the framework catches that error higher up and turns it into a redirect response.

That means your catch block receives it first. Your code swallows the redirect, returns { error: ... }, and the framework never sees it.

The same is true for notFound(), which also works by throwing. Both are written to stop execution immediately, which is why TypeScript treats them as functions that never return.

Why It Is Hard to Catch

  • The data is saved. The only visible symptom is a wrong error message, so it looks like a UI bug, not a logic bug.
  • It is inconsistent in your head. The same redirect() works fine outside a try, so you assume it is fine everywhere.
  • Your logs are confusing. If you log the caught error, you will see a strange error with a NEXT_REDIRECT digest and think something crashed.
  • It tempts you to retry. Users see an error, submit again and create duplicates.

Fix 1: Keep redirect() Outside the try Block

Only wrap the code that can genuinely fail, and redirect afterwards:

export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
  let postId: string;

  try {
    const post = await db.post.create({
      data: { title: String(formData.get('title')) },
    });
    postId = post.id;
  } catch (err) {
    return { error: 'Could not create post' };
  }

  redirect(`/posts/${postId}`);
}

The try now covers only the database call. If it fails, you return the error. If it succeeds, execution continues to redirect(), which is outside any catch, so it can do its job.

This is the cleanest option, and it is the one I use by default.

Fix 2: Rethrow If You Must Catch Everything

Sometimes the redirect() sits deep inside a helper, and restructuring is awkward. Then let the framework's own errors pass through your catch. Newer Next.js versions provide a helper for exactly this:

import { redirect, unstable_rethrow } from 'next/navigation';

try {
  // ...work that may call redirect() or notFound() somewhere inside
} catch (err) {
  unstable_rethrow(err); // lets redirect/notFound errors continue upward
  return { error: 'Something went wrong' };
}

The name says it is not final, so check the documentation for the version you use. If it is not available in yours, structure your code as in Fix 1.

Fix 3: Do Not Use Catch-All to Control Flow

A broader habit helps here. A catch (err) with no check is a very wide net. Catch what you expect:

catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof DuplicateTitleError) {
    return { error: 'You already have a post with that title' };
  }
  throw err; // anything else is not yours to handle here
}

Rethrowing what you do not recognize means the framework's own signals, real crashes and bugs all reach the place that is meant to handle them.

Where Else This Bites

  • notFound() inside try. A missing record becomes your generic error instead of a 404 page.
  • Route handlers and Server Components. The same rule applies: any try/catch around a call that can redirect or 404 will swallow it.
  • .catch() on a promise. somePromise.catch(() => null) has the same effect if the promise's code calls redirect().
  • Wrapper functions. A helper like withErrorHandling(fn) that catches everything will break redirects in every function it wraps.

Quick Checklist

Situation What to do
redirect() after a database write Put the write in try, redirect() after it
notFound() when a record is missing Call it outside the try, or rethrow
A shared error-handling wrapper Make it rethrow framework errors
Unsure Catch specific error types, rethrow the rest

The Rule

redirect() and notFound() signal by throwing, so a catch around them will eat the signal. Keep them outside try blocks, or rethrow what you do not recognize.

Quick audit: search your project for redirect( and notFound(. For each hit, look upward. If it sits inside a try, you have either a bug now or one waiting for the day the code path is used.

Get the templates: https://pixelanas.gumroad.com

Have you ever shipped a form that showed an error after it had succeeded? Tell me in the comments how long it took you to find it.

articles.title: Why JavaScript Silently Changes Large JSON Numbers
articles.description: JSON.parse rounds integers above 2^53 without an error. A reproducible example, why it happens, how to detect it, and how to read big IDs exactly.
articles.body_html:
JavaScript can silently change large integers when it parses perfectly valid JSON. That matters for database IDs, API responses, and the tools you use to look at them. Run this in Node or a browser console:

const order = JSON.parse('{"orderId": 9007199254740993, "amount": 1.50}');
console.log(order.orderId);
console.log(JSON.stringify(order));

Output:

9007199254740992
{"orderId":9007199254740992,"amount":1.5}

The ID is now off by one. There's no exception and no warning, and the result is still valid JSON. If you pass that ID to the next request, you're asking about a different order.

Where the digit goes

JSON's grammar puts no limit on the size of a number. JSON.parse does: it turns every number into a JavaScript Number, which is an IEEE 754 double. A double has a 53-bit significand, so every integer up to 2^53 − 1 is stored exactly:

Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER // 9007199254740991

Above that, only some integers fit. Between 2^53 and 2^54, a double can only hold even integers. 9007199254740993 is odd, so it's rounded to a neighbour, 9007199254740992. The same thing happens to the literal in your source code, before any JSON is involved:

9007199254740993 === 9007199254740992 // true

Further up the range the gaps get wider, so the error gets bigger:

JSON.parse('{"big": 12345678901234567890}').big // 12345678901234567000

Not every large integer changes: 9007199254740992 is stored exactly. The trouble is that you can't tell from the parsed value whether it was rounded.

Two related changes come from the same step. 1.50 comes back as 1.5: the value is the same, but once it's a Number there's no record of the trailing zero, so JSON.stringify can't reproduce what you sent. And a number too large for a double becomes Infinity, which JSON can't represent, so it's written out as null:

JSON.stringify(JSON.parse('{"d": 1e400}')) // '{"d":null}'
JSON input After JSON.parse + JSON.stringify What changed
9007199254740993 9007199254740992 Integer rounded
12345678901234567890 12345678901234567000 Integer rounded
1.50 1.5 Trailing zero dropped, value unchanged
1e400 null Too large: parsed as Infinity, which JSON can't represent
"9007199254740993" "9007199254740993" Nothing: strings are kept as written

JSON itself doesn't limit number size. RFC 8259 lets implementations set their own limits, and notes that integers between −(2^53 − 1) and 2^53 − 1 are the ones every implementation using double-precision numbers will agree on. The rounding comes from JavaScript's Number, not from JSON.

What's usually affected

  • 64-bit integer IDs (BIGINT) once their values pass 2^53, for example IDs generated from timestamps or random bits rather than a small counter.
  • Snowflake-style IDs. X (Twitter) and Discord both use them, and both are far above 2^53.
  • Numbers produced by backends with native 64-bit integers. The server serializes them correctly; the precision is lost only when JavaScript parses them.

Some APIs work around it. Discord's API reference says snowflakes are always returned as strings in the HTTP API, to avoid integer overflow in some languages. Twitter's API returned every ID twice, as the number id and the string id_str, and its documentation told JavaScript developers to use id_str.

Checking whether a value may have been rounded

After parsing, Number.isSafeInteger tells you whether an integer is inside the exact range:

Number.isSafeInteger(order.orderId) // false
Number.isSafeInteger(9007199254740991) // true

false means the value may have been rounded, not that it was: 9007199254740992 is itself representable. To know for sure you need the original text, and newer runtimes give it to you. The reviver function passed to JSON.parse now receives a third argument, context, whose source property is the number exactly as it was written. This comes from the TC39 proposal JSON.parse source text access, which is at Stage 4.

This function finds integers outside JavaScript's safe integer range and shows their original text alongside the parsed value:

function unsafeIntegers(text) {
  const found = [];
  JSON.parse(text, (key, value, context) => {
    if (typeof value === 'number' && Number.isInteger(value) && !Number.isSafeInteger(value))
      found.push({ key, source: context.source, parsed: value });
    return value;
  });
  return found;
}

unsafeIntegers('{"id": 9007199254740993, "user": {"id": 42}, "ids": [12345678901234567890]}');

Output in Node 23:

[
  { key: 'id', source: '9007199254740993', parsed: 9007199254740992 },
  {
    key: '0',
    source: '12345678901234567890',
    parsed: 12345678901234567000
  }
]

The second key is '0' because the value is the first element of the ids array. In runtimes that don't support the proposal, context is undefined, so check your target environments before relying on it.

Keeping large integers exact

Send them as strings. If you control the API, "orderId": "9007199254740993" is the most robust fix, because it works in every client and language. This is what Discord does.

Convert them in a reviver. This approach requires a runtime that supports JSON.parse source text access. With it, you can turn a specific field into a BigInt:

const text = '{"orderId": 9007199254740993, "amount": 1.50}';
const exact = JSON.parse(text, (key, value, context) =>
  key === 'orderId' ? BigInt(context.source) : value);

exact.orderId // 9007199254740993n

JSON.stringify refuses to write a BigInt:

TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt

The same proposal adds JSON.rawJSON, which lets a replacer emit the digits unchanged:

JSON.stringify(exact, (key, value) =>
  typeof value === 'bigint' ? JSON.rawJSON(value.toString()) : value);
// '{"orderId":9007199254740993,"amount":1.5}'

The ID survives the round trip and amount still loses its trailing zero, because the reviver only touched orderId. MDN lists JSON.rawJSON as Baseline 2025, so it's available in current browsers but not in older ones.

Use a parser built for it. Libraries such as json-bigint ("JSON.parse with bigints support") and lossless-json ("Parse JSON without risk of losing numeric information") parse numbers without going through Number. Check how each one represents numbers before choosing; their APIs differ.

A quick test for JSON tools

Formatters, viewers and diff tools often call JSON.parse and JSON.stringify internally. To see whether one does, paste this:

{ "a": 9007199254740993, "b": 12345678901234567890, "c": 1.50, "d": 1e400 }

A tool built on the standard functions gives back:

{"a":9007199254740992,"b":12345678901234567000,"c":1.5,"d":null}

If the numeric text survives unchanged, that's a good sign the tool preserves number precision for this test. It doesn't guarantee every operation is lossless, so test the transformations you actually use.

References

  • MDN: JSON.parse()
  • MDN: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
  • MDN: JSON.rawJSON()
  • TC39: JSON.parse source text access

articles.title: Your AI-built Next.js app stores everything in localStorage? 6 ways it quietly loses data
articles.description: If an AI assistant built your Next.js side project on localStorage, it probably works fine until a...
articles.body_html:
If an AI assistant built your Next.js side project on localStorage, it probably works fine until a corrupt value, a full quota, a second tab, or Safari's 7-day cleanup wipes someone's data without a single error on screen. Here are six checks, each with a tested fix and a prompt you can paste into Cursor, Claude Code, or ChatGPT.

The examples come from a small budget app (expenses, categories, monthly budgets) built prompt by prompt with no backend. Everything below was run in headless Chromium unless it says otherwise.

1. "Return an empty array on bad JSON" deletes the data on the next save

JSON.parse throws on anything malformed, so assistants wrap it and fall back to []. That's the right instinct, and it's what our own test app did. A smoke test confirmed the page shows "No expenses yet" instead of crashing.

The problem is the next line of code that runs. The user adds an expense, the app pushes it onto that empty array and saves. In our test, a truncated value with two records, [{"id":1},{"id":2}, became [{"id":3}] after one add. The two old records were gone, and nothing ever said so.

Keep the broken value before you replace it:

export function load<T>(key: string): { ok: boolean; items: T[] } {
  if (typeof window === "undefined") return { ok: true, items: [] };
  const raw = localStorage.getItem(key);
  if (raw === null) return { ok: true, items: [] };
  try {
    const parsed = JSON.parse(raw);
    if (Array.isArray(parsed)) return { ok: true, items: parsed as T[] };
  } catch {
    // fall through and keep a copy below
  }
  localStorage.setItem(`${key}:corrupt-${Date.now()}`, raw); // keep the evidence
  return { ok: false, items: [] };
}

When ok is false, show a banner ("Some saved data couldn't be read. A copy was kept.") so the user knows to export before adding more.

In lib/storage.ts, when a stored value is missing, return []. When it's present but invalid JSON or not an array, copy the raw string to <key>:corrupt-<timestamp> before returning [], and return a flag so the page can show a warning banner. Never overwrite a value you couldn't parse without keeping a copy.

2. setItem can throw, and the UI keeps pretending it saved

MDN puts localStorage at up to 5 MiB per origin, and setItem throws QuotaExceededError when you go over. In our test, writing values of a million characters each, the fifth setItem threw:

QuotaExceededError: Failed to execute 'setItem' on 'Storage':
Setting the value of 'big4' exceeded the quota.

A text-only budget app takes a long time to get there. Add something like receipt photos as base64 strings and you'll get there much sooner. The usual AI-generated code updates React state first and calls setItem after, with no try/catch. The new row shows up on screen and is gone on refresh.

Make every save report whether it worked, and only update the UI from storage:

export function save<T>(key: string, items: T[]): boolean {
  try {
    localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(items));
    return true;
  } catch {
    window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("app:storage-error", {
      detail: "Could not save. Storage may be full.",
    }));
    return false;
  }
}

Our test app does exactly this, with a small banner component that listens for the event.

Wrap every localStorage.setItem in try/catch and return true or false. On failure, dispatch a window event, and add a layout-level banner that listens for it and says "Could not save. Storage may be full." After saving, reload the list from storage instead of trusting the state you just set.

3. Every project on localhost:3000 shares one storage

Storage belongs to an origin, which is scheme plus hostname plus port. Your budget app, last week's todo app, and the tutorial you cloned yesterday all ran on http://localhost:3000, so they all read and write the same localStorage.

In our test, a second tab on the same host and port saw a key set by the first. A tab on port 3082 saw nothing, and so did 127.0.0.1 on the same port, because that's a different hostname. Then localStorage.clear() from one "project" also wiped an unrelated theme key.

Two rules fix this. Prefix every key with the app name (vibe-budget:expenses, not expenses). And never call localStorage.clear() in a "Reset data" button. Remove only your own keys:

Object.keys(localStorage)
  .filter((k) => k.startsWith("vibe-budget:") && k !== "vibe-budget:theme")
  .forEach((k) => localStorage.removeItem(k));

In the test, that removed the app's data and left both other-app:todos and the saved theme alone.

Every localStorage key in this project must start with <app-name>:. Never call localStorage.clear(). "Clear all data" removes only keys with our prefix, keeps the theme key, then re-seeds defaults.

4. Two open tabs overwrite each other

Most generated pages load data once in useEffect, keep it in state, and save the whole array from state on every change. Open the app in two tabs and that becomes last-write-wins with stale data.

We reproduced it with two tabs. Tab B added an item and saved. Tab A, still holding the old array in memory, added its own item and saved. B's item disappeared.

Two small changes cover it. First, read the latest value from storage right before you write, instead of saving whatever is in state:

function addExpense(e: Expense) {
  const current = loadExpenses(); // re-read, don't trust state
  saveExpenses([...current, e]);
  setExpenses(loadExpenses());
}

With that change the same test kept all three items. Second, listen for the storage event so the other tab refreshes:

useEffect(() => {
  const onStorage = (ev: StorageEvent) => {
    if (ev.key?.startsWith("vibe-budget:")) setExpenses(loadExpenses());
  };
  window.addEventListener("storage", onStorage);
  return () => window.removeEventListener("storage", onStorage);
}, []);

The storage event fires in the other tabs of the same origin, not in the tab that made the change. Our test confirmed that, so don't count on it to refresh the tab doing the writing.

Every add, edit, or delete must read the current array from storage, apply the change, save it, then reload state from storage. Also add a storage event listener on each page that reloads its data when a key with our prefix changes in another tab.

5. Import accepts the file, but not safely

Export/import is the only backup a localStorage app has, so it's worth checking twice. Our test app does the basics well: it checks that expenses, categories, and budgets are arrays with the right field types, rejects a bad file, and leaves existing data untouched. Export, clear site data, refresh, import, and everything came back.

Two gaps were still there when we read the code. The export writes version: 1, but import never looks at it. So the day you rename a field, an old backup will either fail validation or, worse, pass it. And import writes three keys one after another without checking whether each save worked. If the second write hits the quota, you end up with new categories and old expenses.

In import: reject files whose version is missing or higher than the current one, and run a migrate(data, fromVersion) step for older versions. Before writing anything, keep a copy of the current data in memory. Save all three keys, check each save() result, and if any fails, restore the copy and show an error.

6. Safari deletes it after 7 days without a visit

This is the one you can't fix in code. WebKit's tracking prevention deletes all of a site's script-writable storage, localStorage included, "after seven days of Safari use without user interaction on the site." MDN describes the same proactive eviction and notes that only Safari does it. A web app added to the Home Screen has its own day counter, so it isn't affected the same way.

So a Safari user who forgets your budget app for a week and a half can come back to an empty app. Private windows are worse: their localStorage is gone when the last private tab closes.

The honest fix is to tell users and make backups easy:

  • Say in the UI and README that data lives only in this browser, and recommend Export.
  • Show "Last backup: never" or a date on the settings page, and nudge after a week.
  • If you can't afford to lose the data, it needs a server. That's a different app.

Add a "Data is stored only in this browser" note on the settings page with an Export button next to it. Store the date of the last export under <app-name>:lastExport and show it. If it's more than 7 days old or missing, show a small reminder to export.

Put the rules where the assistant reads them every time

Ten prompts in, an assistant may no longer follow storage rules you gave it back in prompt 3. Put them in AGENTS.md or .cursor/rules/storage.mdc (with alwaysApply: true) so they're loaded on every request:

Storage rules:
- All keys start with "vibe-budget:". Never call localStorage.clear().
- Never overwrite a value you couldn't parse; back it up first.
- setItem is always in try/catch and returns true/false.
- Read from storage right before every write; reload state after.
- Finish every change with: npm run lint && npm run build

Then test the failure paths on purpose. Put {corrupt in a key from DevTools and reload. Open two tabs and add something in each. Clear site data and import your last export. If you only test the happy path, you won't find any of these bugs.

If you want to see the storage layer prompt our test app was built from, it's prompt 3 in the free Vibe Budget App sample, along with the scaffold, types, seed data, and navigation prompts. It covers the parse fallback and prefixed keys, not the corrupt-value backup from section 1, so add that line yourself.
